articles.body_html:
This is going to cover a lot, and I will do my best to keep it brief. Thank you for following the journey of an independent artist powering through the web. Small, but mighty. ⚡

Last night I had one of those nights where my brain just refused to shut off, despite being tired. This is pretty rare for me, I like the peace that comes with sleeping, and the bed can be a very strong magnet.

Before I fell asleep, I decided I was a project manager, and that my entire strategy needed a facelift.

As solo developer, I leaned into claude to sort out my 9,000 thoughts.

🏹 Strengths: Creativity, drive, ideas, writing, communication, time management, learning, technical skills, inspiring others, general management, and life administration.

⬇️ Weaknesses: Deviating from plans, emotions, self doubt, and other anxieties

👾 Claudinarian

Something clicked in my brain last night. I thought to myself: “This project is so vast that I need A project manager and another developer so that I can run things.” 🤣I sat with that idea for a bit, feeling overwhelmed. I gave some thought to what my real issues were on a very deep and personal level. I reflected on my own existence.

I decided to organize my thoughts with Claude, as is my go-to. I have become quite the claudinarian. Having messed with the “Projects” feature of claude before, the multi-agent bot with an orchestrator at the top, I knew the most appropriate manner to share my thoughts. I had previously gotten lost with this feature in the sub-bots and frequently lost my place and it was very confusing. Having that experience I knew I had to approach claude with targeted, specific and detailed requests. This way, claude would send a minion to do the bidding. Once that started, I could return to claude boss to place a new request. I think I’ve got it figured out now, I won't navigate to a minion and try to complete a project from a sub-agent (Guilty!)

As each task completed, I had Claude build me and artifact for that area of focus. I was creating and collecting organized documentation for myself so I could build a legitimate project plan with enough work to keep me busy for literally weeks.

How it started

The original plan was to optimize SEO, after having been absolutely devastated by my website performance (yes, I felt like a failure for a second “wow, how do I suck that bad? I try so hard!”) 😂

In my previous post, I shared a redirect disaster created from years of doing things on the web for my business as a non-developer. I had made a giant mess for myself. I’m sure if I went to a 'professional' they would have said something like “Here is the rebranding plan for your new business…” not wanting to deal with my disaster. Good thing I started learning web development a few years ago! I have gained so many skills that will be useful for running my small business. Monumentally powerful and not something that too many CEOs can say they can do themselves. Maniacal Laughter

Side tangent again. 😂 pivot Too many redirects in my brain.

First Task

SO, I have boss claude and the minion claudettes doing some legwork. This is my team for the night. Before I created the first task, I did some personal research. After fixing the redirect problem, I investigated my accessibility features to keep it clean. (I had recently completed a formal webdev class and the accessibility stuff was fresh in my head). everfluorescent.com came out mostly good, but I created a To-Do list and added that to it. No big deal, I can handle that.

With redirects created properly, canonical set as it should be and a decent user-friendliness score, I proceeded to run everfluorescent.com through multiple SEO checkers. They returned mixed results as expected. Here is some free ones I used that you may find useful:

  • SEOptimizer (Full audit)
  • Open Graph Preview Tool (Found no share image)
  • SEObility.net (Came back with on-page score of 87%)
  • SavageAudit (85/100 overall - details locked)

Savage Audit is awesome even on the free tier. Look what it said 🤣

I fed claude the data from all 4 sources, I told it to use it as a reference to build my plan.

This morning, I still had a bajillion tabs open and I noticed something. Before implementing the next wave of SEO optimization (not the first time I’m doing this), my average rank in searches was at position 5.3. 5.3!!!! That’s the first page of a Google Search! Boss.

My indexing is currently being fixed as well. As you can see from the chart below, the trends are now moving in the right direction. Redirects improving, proper canonical tag, and 404s have trended downward as well. This is excellent news.

Second Task

Diving into the problem of reach is next. This is something that I am not surprised about. Due to personal reasons, I had basically ghosted all of my social medias for the last few years. This is a significant area of pain for my brand and shop. (This was one of those situations where personal life disintegrated work life, I would always get compliments at live events, and it was very difficult to stop doing it.) I came up with a plan to create 365 days of unique content. Posting will be set to semi automatic. This will undoubtedly be a tremendous amount of work, but luckily I am mostly ready to take on the challenge.

Before I do that I will collect all of my information from wherever it lives, and I will have lots of stories to tell and share with the world about my brand, experiences, and travels. I'm not sure what provoked me at midnight last night. Perhaps a small inner voice silently screaming: "Move woman! You can cover a lot of ground quickly now!"

Third Task

Rebranding and breathing life back into a business is no easy task, that is what the importance of the regular scheduled content creation is. The plan is to cleanup security and management features on all social medias (I did this a while back, but it's going to get rechecked and updated with a tedious checklist!) I will use an external free tool for scheduled content posting. (Metricool fits the bill at the moment) This way, I can rest assured that my brand and content is being shared without needing to take so much time out everyday for posting and managing social media.

24 hours of evidence!

With some of the most severe issues addressed, It appears that I am already heading in the right direction! The chart does not lie.

I just checked my Google analytics and here is the story:

Things are looking up, and we are getting back on the right track. I've still got a monumental amount of work to do, but one thing at a time. I don't want to get excited over some 'blip anomaly' and I'm going to watch it like an obsessed hawk for a while.

Man, I'm so pleased to see that line finally peeled itself off the floor in google analytics!

Thank you for sharing my excitement and reading my post! <3

articles.title: MAYHEM: A Monster-Collecting Battle Game built with AdaL and Cloudinary ⚔️
articles.description: Create your legend. Collect the extraordinary. Fight for glory.  What if you could upload an image,...
articles.body_html:
Create your legend. Collect the extraordinary. Fight for glory.

What if you could upload an image, turn it into a collectible monster, build a squad of three, and take it into a turn-based battle?

That idea became MAYHEM — Monster Fighting Arena, an open-source browser game where you collect creatures, create your own fighters from images, and battle rival tamers in a dark-fantasy world.

I built MAYHEM using AdaL, an AI-assisted development workflow, and integrated Cloudinary to handle monster artwork uploads, image transformations, optimized delivery, and shareable collectible cards. Here’s a look at the project, the technology behind it, and what you can explore in the game.

🎮 What is MAYHEM?

MAYHEM is a browser-based monster-collecting and turn-based battle game. It runs on desktop, tablet, and mobile without requiring installation or an account. The core idea is simple:

  • Collect: Discover monsters across six elemental types and four rarity tiers.
  • Create: Upload an image and transform it into a custom monster.
  • Build: Assemble a team of three monsters.
  • Battle: Fight opponents using attacks, special abilities, defensive moves, items, and team switching.
  • Progress: Earn coins and XP, unlock new species, complete quests, and improve your monsters.

The game combines collectible-card mechanics with RPG-style progression and turn-based combat.

✨ Explore the game

1. Discover: Enter the arena

The home screen introduces the world of MAYHEM through a cinematic fantasy scene, animated effects, featured discoveries, daily rewards, and progression information.

The interface uses a dark purple atmosphere, glowing accents, and fiery orange calls to action to create an arcade-inspired fantasy experience.

2. Collection: Build your bestiary

Every monster has its own identity, elemental type, rarity, stats, and special ability.

The collection includes four rarity tiers:

  • Common
  • Rare
  • Epic
  • Legendary

You can search for monsters, filter by element or rarity, sort your collection, and mark favourites. Higher rarity cards can feature foil and holographic-style finishes.

3. Create Your Monster: Turn images into fighters

This is one of my favourite parts of the project.

Instead of choosing only from predefined creatures, players can upload an image, drag and drop a file, paste an image, or use bundled sample artwork. They can then customize the monster's name, element, and rarity, choose a battle style, and preview its collectible card before creating it. The creation studio also includes generated stats, special abilities, and a full-screen reveal when a new monster is born.

4. Battle Arena: Strategy matters

Players select a squad of three monsters and face rival tamers in turn-based battles.

Available actions include:

  • Attack: Deal damage to the opponent.
  • Special: Use a powerful monster ability.
  • Defend: Reduce incoming damage and gain defensive benefits.
  • Switch: Change the active monster.
  • Items: Use available battle items.

Combat also includes elemental matchups, speed-based turn order, critical hits, status effects, shields, and buffs. The arena has three difficulty tiers, each with its own setting: Verdant Ruins, Stormspire Citadel, and Infernal Throne.

5. Progression and Shop: Keep getting stronger

Battles and quests feed into the game's progression system. Players earn XP and coins, level up their summoner, unlock additional monster species, purchase stat boosts, learn skills, and acquire battle items. Achievements, collection milestones, daily quests, and login streaks provide more goals beyond simply winning fights.

🤖 Building with AdaL

MAYHEM was designed and developed with AdaL, an AI-assisted development workflow. AdaL helped with several parts of the project, including game design, UI and UX, the battle engine, procedural audio, and Cloudinary integration.

A project like this requires more than generating a few screens. The interface, game rules, monster stats, battle actions, progression, image uploads, and saved state all need to work together. That made MAYHEM an opportunity to bring several pieces into one playable experience rather than build a static mockup.

☁️ How Cloudinary powers MAYHEM

Monster creation depends on images, so image handling is a core part of the experience—not just an extra feature.

I integrated Cloudinary to manage monster artwork and make it suitable for different parts of the game.

Here's how it is used:

Cloudinary capability How MAYHEM uses it
Unsigned uploads Upload monster artwork directly from the browser using an upload preset
Image transformations Crop and resize images for collectible cards and thumbnails
Automatic format and quality Use f_auto,q_auto for optimized image delivery
Smart cropping Use c_fill,g_auto to fill the card frame while focusing on the subject
Optional background removal Use e_background_removal when the required add-on is available
Shareable card images Render monster details, rarity, stats, abilities, and borders into shareable cards
CDN delivery Load artwork at responsive sizes with lazy loading and fallbacks

For example, the transformation settings can request an automatically selected format and quality:

f_auto,q_auto

For a card image that needs to fill a portrait frame while keeping the main subject in focus:

c_fill,g_auto

These transformations help serve artwork in a form suited to the game's collectible cards.

A small but important security detail

The browser uses an unsigned upload preset and browser-safe Cloudinary configuration. The Cloudinary API secret is never exposed through a VITE_ environment variable.

Game data—such as monster stats, inventory, progression, and battle rules—remains separate from image hosting. Cloudinary handles the images, while the game handles the gameplay.

MAYHEM also has a fallback: if Cloudinary isn't configured, the game can process uploaded artwork in the browser and save it on the device. It reports that fallback rather than pretending a cloud upload succeeded.

🛠️ Tech stack

The project uses:

  • React 18 — UI and reusable components
  • TypeScript 5 — typed game data and application logic
  • Vite 5 — development server and production build
  • Tailwind CSS 4 — styling and interface design
  • Cloudinary — image uploads, transformations, and delivery
  • Web Audio API — procedural music and sound effects
  • localStorage — local game saves and player progression
  • AdaL — AI-assisted development workflow

The game logic is organized into modules for elements, monster data, stats, combat rules, turn order, progression, and persistence. The UI is divided into screens and reusable components.

🌱 What's next?

MAYHEM is open source under the MIT License. The project can be forked, modified, reskinned, and extended.

Some areas where contributors could help include:

  • Adding new monsters, elements, and abilities
  • Improving battle balance
  • Online Multiplayer
  • Creating new arena environments
  • Improving accessibility and translations
  • Exploring a real backend for persistent player accounts and shared progression

The current game saves progress locally through localStorage, with a storage adapter that can support a future backend implementation.

🤝 Try it, fork it, improve it

MAYHEM brings together creature collection, image-driven customization, turn-based combat, progression systems, and cloud-powered image handling in one browser game.

I'm especially interested in the possibilities of letting players create their own creatures instead of being limited to a predefined roster. If you're interested in game development, AI-assisted coding, React, or Cloudinary image workflows, I'd love for you to explore the project.

Project repository: https://github.com/ab2030909/MAYHEM-monsters-card-game
Website Link: https://mayhem-monsters.vercel.app/

Built with: AdaL + React + TypeScript + Cloudinary

If you check it out, let me know: what kind of monster would you create first? 🔥

⚔️ Enter the arena. Unleash MAYHEM.

articles.title: I Coded for 30 Days Using Only Claude Code — Here's What I Learned
articles.description: Not "AI-assisted." Not "copilot suggestions I edited." I made a rule: for 30 days I don't type...
articles.body_html:
Not "AI-assisted." Not "copilot suggestions I edited." I made a rule: for 30 days I don't type application code. The AI does. My job is to describe, review, and approve.

I shipped a real product this way — a small SaaS with auth, Stripe billing, a dashboard, and a public API. It works. It's in production. And along the way I found out exactly where the "AI writes everything now" dream holds up and where it quietly falls apart.

This isn't a hype post and it isn't a doom post. It's a field report.

The rules

To keep myself honest:

  1. I don't write application logic by hand. I prompt, the AI writes.
  2. I can read every line, reject it, and ask again — but I can't fix it myself in the editor.
  3. Config, secrets, and "click the button in the dashboard" steps are mine (the AI can't do those anyway).
  4. If I get truly stuck for more than an hour, I log it as a "break" and write the code myself.

By the end I had 9 logged breaks. Those breaks are the interesting part.

What worked shockingly well

Let me be fair to the machine first, because a lot of this genuinely surprised me.

Greenfield scaffolding is basically solved. "Set up a Next.js app with Postgres, Drizzle, and auth" — done, correctly, in one shot. The first 40% of the project flew by faster than I've ever built anything.

Boilerplate it never gets wrong. CRUD endpoints, form validation, Zod schemas, a table with sorting and pagination. The stuff I hate writing, produced perfectly, every time, no notes.

It's a phenomenal rubber duck. "Why is this query slow?" got me a better answer than I'd have reasoned to alone — it spotted a missing index and an N+1 in the same breath.

For the first week I genuinely thought I'd write the "developers are obsolete" post. Then week two happened.

What broke — the 9 breaks, honestly

Break 1–3: It can't hold the whole system in its head

Brilliant at the file in front of it, blind to the one three folders over. It wrote a second formatCurrency helper because it didn't know the first existed. Re-implemented my auth check inline instead of the middleware I already had. Introduced a subtly different User type in a new module.

None of these are "bugs" — everything compiled, everything passed. They're architecture drift, and architecture drift is invisible until the day it costs you a week.

The AI optimizes locally. Coherence across a system is still a human job.

Break 4–5: It confidently writes plausible, wrong code

The scariest failures weren't crashes. They were code that looked right and ran fine on the happy path.

The billing webhook it wrote acknowledged Stripe events before persisting them. Flawless in testing. In production, one DB blip = a paying customer locked out, no record, no trail. I only caught it because I've been burned by exactly this before. A junior copying this output would not have caught it. That's the part that keeps me up.

Break 6: Debugging its own code is a hall of mirrors

When something broke that the AI couldn't see, asking it to fix it produced changes, not fixes. It would rewrite the function, swear the bug was gone, and reintroduce it two prompts later. Without dropping into the debugger myself to understand the real state, we'd have spun forever. Biggest time sink of the month.

Break 7–8: Taste, and saying "no, less"

Asked for a settings page, it gave me 14 options nobody wanted. Asked for error handling, it wrapped everything in try/catch and swallowed the errors. The AI's instinct is always to add. Knowing what to leave out — the product-design part of engineering — it has none.

Break 9: The last 10% is still 90% of the work

"Demo works" took a week. "Handles a real user doing something weird at 2am" took the other three. Edge cases, race conditions, the empty state, the error state, the double-click state — the AI does none of it unless you know to ask, and knowing to ask is the job.

The uncomfortable synthesis

AI didn't replace me. It replaced the *tasks I used to give juniors.* The scaffolding, the boilerplate, the first draft — the exact work a junior becomes a senior by doing. So if the AI does all the entry-level work, where does the next senior come from? You can't skip the 10,000 hours; you can only move where they're spent.

The skills that mattered every single day were senior ones: knowing the code was subtly wrong, knowing what not to build, holding the whole system in my head to catch the drift. AI didn't flatten the hierarchy — it made the top more valuable and sawed off the ladder to get there.

What I actually changed

I didn't stop using AI — I use it for 100% of the typing now and always will. I changed the guardrails, and every one maps to a break above:

  • The thing that writes the code is never the thing that reviews it. A separate reviewer, prompted to refute the diff, catches the plausible-but-wrong code the author always waves through.
  • Nothing merges without a human who can see the blast radius the model can't.
  • "It compiles and the tests pass" is the start of review, not the end — the model writes tests that agree with its own wrong mental model.

Author here, skeptic there, human on the merge button — that separation is the whole reason I could hand the typing to a machine and still sleep. It's also exactly how we build xenition: agents that do the work, a different agent that tries to tear it down, and a person who owns the decision.

Would I do it again?

For a prototype? In a heartbeat — I'd never scaffold by hand again. For production? AI for 100% of the typing and 0% of the thinking. The typing was never the hard part. It just felt like it was.

articles.title: You're Debouncing Scroll Wrong. requestAnimationFrame Fixes It.
articles.description: Debouncing a scroll handler makes it wait until scrolling stops — which is why your sticky header always lags half a beat. requestAnimationFrame fixes the lag by syncing updates to the browser's own paint clock instead of a timer.
articles.body_html:
Our sticky header started lagging behind the scroll by about half a second. Not broken — just late, like it was watching the page over a bad video call. Scroll up fast and the header's drop shadow would still be fading in a beat after you'd already stopped.

The code looked right. It was debounced, just like the resize handler two files over, just like every "optimize this event listener" article says to do. Debouncing a scroll handler is the move everyone learns for performance reasons. Nobody mentions it also breaks the thing you were trying to show the user in real time.

The handler that was "optimized" into being wrong

Here's roughly what was wrapping the scroll listener:

function debounce(fn, wait) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), wait);
  };
}

window.addEventListener("scroll", debounce(updateHeader, 150));

debounce resets its timer on every single scroll event and only fires once the events stop coming — once you stop scrolling. That's exactly what you want for a resize handler recalculating a layout: you don't care about every intermediate width, just the final one, and recalculating 40 times mid-drag is wasted work.

A sticky header isn't that. The user wants to see the shadow and background opacity change as they scroll, not 150ms after they've already arrived. Debounce doesn't throttle the rate of updates — it delays the update until the interaction is over. For anything the user is supposed to watch happen live, that's backwards.

Quick gut check before you keep reading: have you ever debounced a scroll or mousemove handler because that's just "what you do" for frequent events, without asking whether debounce or throttle was the one you actually needed?

Throttling fixes the lag. It doesn't fix the timing.

The standard next move is to swap debounce for throttle — run the handler on a fixed interval instead of waiting for silence:

function throttle(fn, wait) {
  let last = 0;
  return (...args) => {
    const now = Date.now();
    if (now - last >= wait) {
      last = now;
      fn(...args);
    }
  };
}

window.addEventListener("scroll", throttle(updateHeader, 16));

This is closer — the header updates during the scroll now. But look at that 16. Where did it come from? It's "roughly one frame at 60Hz," typed in because that's the number every blog post uses. It assumes the display is 60Hz. A lot of phones and newer monitors run at 90Hz, 120Hz, even 144Hz — on those, 16 isn't "once per frame" anymore, it's "slower than the screen can actually paint," and the update looks subtly behind even though your throttle is technically running.

You're also still paying for a Date.now() call and a comparison on every scroll event, even the ones you throw away. The scroll event itself can fire dozens of times between two paints. All of that extra firing is wasted — the browser is only going to show the user a new frame once, no matter how many times you ran your handler before it.

The browser already has a clock for this

Here's the part that's easy to miss: the browser knows exactly when it's about to paint the next frame. You don't have to estimate it with a setTimeout interval — you can ask for it directly with requestAnimationFrame.

let ticking = false;

function onScroll() {
  if (ticking) return;
  ticking = true;
  requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    updateHeader();
    ticking = false;
  });
}

window.addEventListener("scroll", onScroll, { passive: true });

The ticking flag is the whole trick. scroll can fire many times before the next paint; the flag makes sure only the first one of those schedules an update, and every scroll event after it until the next frame is a no-op — a single boolean check, nothing more. When the browser is finally ready to paint, it calls your callback once, you update the header with the latest scroll position, and you flip the flag back so the next scroll event can schedule the next frame.

No guessed interval. No wasted setTimeout calls that get cleared before they fire. No lag after the user stops, because there's no waiting-for-silence step at all — the update rides along with the very next frame the browser was already going to paint, on a 60Hz screen or a 120Hz one.

{ passive: true } is still worth keeping on the listener, but be precise about why: scroll itself isn't cancelable, so preventDefault() inside a scroll handler does nothing either way — passive or not. The option earns its keep on events that are cancelable, like touchmove and wheel, where it tells the browser you'll never call preventDefault() so it can start scrolling immediately instead of waiting to find out. Add it to the scroll listener anyway as the correct default for any handler that never cancels anything.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

When you still want debounce

None of this makes debounce wrong in general — it just means the choice depends on what the user is waiting for. A search-as-you-type box should wait for the person to stop typing. A "save draft" call should wait for a pause in edits. A window-resize recalculation that's expensive should wait until the user's done dragging the edge of the browser.

The question that decides it: does the user need to see this update during the interaction, or only after it settles? Live visual feedback — scroll position, drag position, pointer tracking — wants a per-frame throttle, and requestAnimationFrame is the native, interval-free way to get one. Anything that's expensive and only matters at the end wants debounce.

The header stopped lagging the day we swapped the setTimeout number for a question the browser could just answer itself.

What's debounced in your codebase right now that's actually supposed to be live? Go check your scroll and mousemove handlers — I'd bet at least one of them is waiting for silence when it should be riding the next frame.

articles.title: Getting Your First 10 Users Is Harder Than Building the Product (Or Is It?)
articles.description: TL;DR: Building proves you can create a solution. Finding users proves the solution matters to...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR: Building proves you can create a solution. Finding users proves the solution matters to someone. These are separate questions, and finishing the first never answers the second.

Reading time: about 12 minutes. For developers and first-time founders.

A developer can spend six months building a product without having to convince a single stranger to care about it.

The code either works or it doesn't. A bug can be investigated. A slow query can be measured. If a feature breaks, there's usually somewhere to start looking.

Then the product is ready, the landing page is live, and the founder starts reaching out to people.

Nothing happens.

A few people visit the website. Someone says the idea sounds interesting. A friend offers encouragement. Perhaps a handful of people create accounts, but nobody returns the following week.

Suddenly, the problem that seemed straightforward during development becomes difficult to explain. The product exists. The founder believes it solves a real problem. Yet the people who supposedly need it aren't showing up.

This is where a familiar piece of startup advice enters the conversation: getting your first ten users is harder than building the product.

There is a reason the advice resonates, especially with developers who are building their first businesses. But it also leaves an important question unanswered.

The real question

Is finding those first ten users actually harder than building the product, or does it feel harder because founders have less control over what happens next?

The distinction matters. If you misunderstand why people aren't using your product, you can spend months trying to solve the wrong problem.

Jump to a section
  1. Building gives you feedback. Selling gives you silence.
  2. Stripe's early customers didn't arrive through a signup page
  3. Ten signups can still mean zero real users
  4. When the advice is right, and when it isn't
  5. A quiet launch can mean four different things
  6. What should you actually do to find the first ten?
  7. The first ten are not the finish line

1. Building gives you feedback. Selling gives you silence.

Consider what happens when a developer encounters a difficult technical problem.

The solution might take hours, days, or even weeks. But there is usually a way to investigate it. You can inspect the logs, reproduce the failure, test a different approach, and gradually narrow down the possibilities.

Progress isn't guaranteed, but the work often produces information you can use.

Customer acquisition is different.

You send twenty carefully written messages and receive two replies. You publish a detailed explanation of your product and nobody clicks through. You demonstrate a feature to someone who says they would love to use it, then never hear from them again.

You have an outcome, but you don't necessarily know what caused it.

Perhaps the people you contacted don't have the problem. Perhaps they do, but your message arrived at the wrong time. Perhaps the product is useful but switching to it would take too much effort. Perhaps they simply don't trust an unfamiliar founder with something important to their work.

Those explanations require different responses. Silence alone cannot tell you which one is correct.

This is one reason acquisition can feel more frustrating than development. With code, you can often make the next experiment more specific because you understand the system you're investigating. With customers, you are still learning how the system works.

You are learning what people care about, what they already use, what they will pay to change, and what makes them trust a product they have never tried.

And you are learning all of this while trying to persuade them to give you their time.

That is a genuinely difficult problem. But it isn't necessarily a harder problem in every measurable sense. A technically ambitious product might require years of engineering, while a simple product could find its first customers in a few days.

The more useful distinction:

Building tests... Finding customers tests...
The question Can you create the solution? Does the solution matter enough that someone will act on it?
Feedback you get Logs, errors, measurable results Often silence
Who controls the outcome Mostly you Mostly other people

Those are separate questions, and finishing the first does not answer the second.

2. Stripe's early customers didn't arrive through a signup page

In his 2013 essay Do Things That Don't Scale, Paul Graham describes how Patrick and John Collison acquired early users for Stripe.1

When somebody agreed to try the payment integration, the brothers wouldn't simply send a link and wait. They would ask to borrow the person's laptop and help install it immediately.

Y Combinator came to call this the "Collison installation."

The approach seems almost excessive now. Why should a founder personally install a product when the whole point of software is to make the experience repeatable?

Because the founders were solving a problem that a signup page couldn't solve for them.

A person who agrees to try a product has made a relatively inexpensive commitment. They can change their mind without consequence. Actually installing it requires more effort and brings the product into contact with the person's real workflow.

By helping with the installation, the founders removed friction and discovered what happened when someone tried to use Stripe for real.

Context matters. Stripe was addressing a concrete problem for developers and businesses, and its early founders had access to a network of potential customers through the startup ecosystem. Their approach does not prove that every product can acquire customers by offering personal onboarding.

It does show something more practical: sometimes the obstacle between interest and usage is not a lack of awareness. It is the work required to get started.

What that looks like in practice:

  • Developer tool: help someone integrate it
  • Software for accountants: import a customer's existing data
  • A service: deliver the first result personally before asking for a longer commitment

These approaches do not scale indefinitely. That is precisely why they can be valuable at the beginning.

Before automating an onboarding process, a founder needs to understand where people struggle with it. Before spending heavily on marketing, they need to know what happens after somebody responds.

The first ten customers can be valuable for the revenue they bring in. They can also reveal problems that a founder working alone would never have discovered.

3. Ten signups can still mean zero real users

There is another problem with the way founders talk about their first users: the word user can describe several very different situations.

  1. Someone visits the landing page.
  2. Someone else joins the waitlist.
  3. A third person creates an account, opens the dashboard, and leaves.

All three might appear in a growth report. None necessarily demonstrates that the product is delivering its promised value.

This distinction is more than a matter of terminology.

In his account of Superhuman's product-market-fit process, founder Rahul Vohra described a company that had spent years building its email product but still needed a clearer way to measure whether users genuinely valued it.2

Superhuman surveyed people who had used the product at least twice in the preceding two weeks. It asked how they would feel if they could no longer use it.

Only 22% said they would be very disappointed.

That result mattered because these weren't simply people who had heard about Superhuman. They had already experienced the product. Yet most did not consider it indispensable.

The team used the survey responses to identify the people who valued the product most, understand what those people appreciated, and make improvements intended to strengthen product-market fit. Vohra subsequently reported that the score rose from 22% to 58%.

- 22%  "very disappointed"  (before)
+ 58%  "very disappointed"  (after)

58%−22%=36 percentage points 58\% - 22\% = 36 \text{ percentage points} 58%−22%=36 percentage points

What this example does and doesn't establish

There are limits to what this example establishes. The survey is a useful diagnostic, not a universal scientific test that can independently prove product-market fit. The results came from Superhuman's particular audience and product, and a high score does not guarantee a sustainable business.

Still, the underlying problem is important.

Getting somebody to sign up and getting somebody to care whether your product disappears are not the same achievement.

For a founder trying to find ten users, this means the milestone needs a definition.

Ten registered accounts might be an appropriate early milestone for testing whether people will respond to an offer. Ten people who repeatedly use a core feature tell you something different. Ten paying customers tell you something different again.

None of those numbers is automatically the right target. The right target depends on what the product is supposed to accomplish.

Product type A meaningful signal might be
Tool used every morning Returning frequently
Quarterly accounting software Completing the quarterly task (daily usage would be a strange expectation)
One-time service Successful completion and willingness to recommend the provider

A founder should measure the behaviour that demonstrates value, rather than assume every product needs the same pattern of engagement.

Read the Superhuman product-market-fit story

4. When the advice is right, and when it isn't

The claim that customer acquisition is harder than building is most convincing when a founder has a working product but no reliable way to reach people who need it.

Imagine a developer who builds a scheduling tool for freelance designers. The technical work is manageable. The product works. But the developer has no existing audience among designers, no relationships with design agencies, and no idea where these freelancers look for tools.

The product might be finished in a month. Finding a group of people willing to try it, learning what they actually need, and discovering whether any of them will pay could take much longer.

The developer isn't necessarily struggling because the product is bad. They are trying to solve a problem for a group of people they don't yet understand well enough.

Now consider a different founder: an accountant who builds a small tool to automate a tedious task that several existing clients already complain about. The founder knows the workflow, has access to the intended users, and can test the tool with people who experience the problem every week.

The technical challenge could be the hardest part of that business. Finding the first few users might be comparatively straightforward.

Developer building for designers Accountant building for own clients
Existing audience No Yes
Knows the workflow No Yes
Likely hardest part Finding users Building the tool

Neither example is unusual enough to support a universal rule. Together, they show why the headline depends on the founder, the market, and the product.

Existing distribution changes the equation, too. Someone with an established audience, a respected reputation in a niche, or a network of potential buyers isn't starting from the same position as someone nobody knows.

That advantage is real. It doesn't mean their product is better, or that their acquisition strategy is automatically repeatable. It means some of the work required to earn attention happened before the product was launched.

The same qualification applies to technically novel products. If a founder doesn't yet know whether a proposed system can work at an acceptable cost, speed, or level of reliability, engineering experiments may need to come first. Talking to potential customers cannot resolve every question about technical feasibility.

The mistake is treating either building or customer acquisition as the correct first step for every startup.

Sometimes the founder needs to write more code. Sometimes they need to speak to potential customers before writing another line. Often, they need to do both, using what they learn from one to inform the other.

5. A quiet launch can mean four different things

Suppose you launch your product and, after several weeks, you still haven't found ten meaningful users.

The tempting response is to do more marketing. Post in more communities. Send more messages. Try another launch platform.

That might help. But first, consider where the process is breaking.

flowchart LR
    A[Launch] --> B{Right people<br/>seeing it?}
    B -- No --> C[1. Reach problem]
    B -- Yes --> D{Taking the<br/>next step?}
    D -- No --> E[2. Offer problem]
    D -- Yes --> F{Reaching the<br/>main benefit?}
    F -- No --> G[3. Activation problem]
    F -- Yes --> H{Returning<br/>or paying?}
    H -- No --> I[4. Retention problem]
    H -- Yes --> J[Keep going]

1. The right people aren't seeing the product

Perhaps the product solves a genuine problem, but your potential customers don't spend time on the channels you're using. Or perhaps you're targeting such a broad audience that your message never feels relevant to anyone in particular.

In this case, changing the product may accomplish very little. You need to understand where the intended customers already look for solutions and how to reach them.

2. People see the product but don't take the next step

This could mean the value proposition is unclear. It could also mean the problem isn't urgent, the price is too high, the proposed solution feels risky, or the person reading your message doesn't have the authority to make a purchase.

It is worth asking what your offer requires someone to believe before they act. An unfamiliar product asking for access to sensitive business data has a much larger trust problem than a free tool that works entirely in the browser.

3. People try the product but never reach its main benefit

Perhaps setup takes too long. Maybe the first screen asks users to configure five things before they can accomplish anything useful. The product might even work exactly as intended, but the value isn't apparent to a new user.

This is where watching someone use the product can reveal more than another round of promotional posts.

4. People get value once but don't return or pay

This is the most uncomfortable possibility because the founder has evidence that the product can work for someone, yet the behaviour isn't continuing.

The problem might be retention, pricing, a low-frequency need, or a mismatch between the person using the product and the person expected to pay. It could also mean the product is useful but not important enough to replace an existing habit.

Not a complete diagnosis. These four categories aren't exhaustive, and the boundaries between them aren't always clean. A confusing product can look like a marketing problem. A weak offer can look like a distribution problem. Low retention can reflect a product that works perfectly but solves a problem people rarely encounter.

The point is not to label every failure immediately.

It is to stop treating every failure as the same failure.

6. What should you actually do to find the first ten?

The best starting point is smaller than a launch campaign.

Choose a specific group of people who already experience the problem your product is intended to solve. Be precise enough that you can identify actual individuals, rather than an enormous category of potential customers.

Then investigate what they do today.

If you're building invoice software for freelancers, find out how those freelancers currently create invoices, follow up on unpaid bills, and keep track of their income. Ask what happens when the process goes wrong. Look for examples of real frustration, time lost, money lost, or workarounds people have already built.

Steve Blank's writing on customer development makes a useful distinction here: founders begin with hypotheses about customers and their needs, then test those hypotheses through conversations and experiments.3 The goal is to discover what is true, not simply to collect encouraging responses.

That means asking about actual behaviour is usually more informative than asking whether somebody likes your idea.

Example: weak evidence vs. strong evidence

A person may tell you they would happily use an invoicing tool. That costs them nothing.

Finding out what they currently use, whether they have paid for alternatives, and whether they'll try your product with a real invoice gives you stronger evidence.

Once you understand the problem, offer a small, concrete next step.

Don't necessarily ask someone to adopt your entire product. Ask whether they'll try one feature, bring one real task into it, or spend twenty minutes showing you how they currently handle the problem.

If the product is ready, help them use it. If it isn't, a prototype or a manually delivered version of the service might be enough to test the underlying assumption, provided you don't misrepresent what you've built.

Track what happens next

Stage What to record
Reached Did the intended person actually see the offer?
Responded Did they reply or ask a meaningful question?
Tried Did they attempt the real task?
Activated Did they reach the product's core value?
Returned Did they use it again when the need arose?
Committed Did they pay, renew, recommend it, or make another meaningful commitment?

Not every product needs all six stages, and not every commitment looks like a payment. The table is a way to make the process observable, not a universal funnel that every business must follow.

Keep notes on why people stop, preferably in their own words. A polite refusal and a detailed objection are not equivalent. Neither is the same as someone who tries the product, gets value from it, and simply doesn't need it again until next month.

Then choose the next experiment based on what you learned:

  • [ ] The wrong people are seeing the offer: change the audience or channel
  • [ ] The right people understand the offer but don't care enough to try it: investigate the problem and the value proposition
  • [ ] They try the product but fail to reach its main benefit: work on that experience
  • [ ] They get value but don't return or pay: investigate the frequency, importance, and economics of the problem

Two weeks can be enough to uncover useful patterns when the target customers are accessible and the product delivers value quickly. It may be nowhere near enough for a business with a long sales cycle or a problem that occurs only a few times a year.

The objective isn't to promise ten users within fourteen days. It is to finish the experiment knowing more than you did when you started.

7. The first ten are not the finish line

There is a reason founders remember their first users. Each one represents a decision that happened outside the codebase: somebody noticed the product, considered it relevant, decided to try it, and perhaps found enough value to return.

But the number ten can be misleading.

Ten users who... ...might tell you
signed up because a friend asked Very little about whether strangers will pay
independently share the same painful problem and pay to solve it A great deal
never return A product problem that another hundred signups would only make harder to ignore

The work isn't finished when the tenth person arrives. That's often when the next question becomes possible.

  • Can you find another ten people with the same problem?
  • Can you reach them through a process you understand?
  • Do they experience enough value to keep using the product?
  • Does acquiring and serving them make economic sense?

Those questions are harder to answer than whether a product can attract ten signups, and they matter more to the future of the business.

So, is getting your first ten users harder than building the product?

Sometimes. Especially when the founder understands the technology but knows very little about the people who might buy it. But the comparison becomes less useful when it turns into a universal rule, or when it encourages founders to treat engineering and customer discovery as competing activities.

A product can be technically excellent and commercially irrelevant. It can also be commercially promising before its engineering is finished. The difficult work is finding out which situation you're in while there is still time to change direction.

That begins with a more useful question than how to get ten users.

Your next question

What would you need to learn from the next person who tries your product to know what to do next?

Share your answer in the comments.

The Startup Café — Real Startup Lessons. Beyond the Hype.

  1. Paul Graham, "Do Things That Don't Scale," 2013. The essay is where the Collison installation story comes from. ↩

  2. Rahul Vohra's account on the First Round Review. The 22% and 58% figures come from Superhuman's own survey of its own users, so treat them as one company's data point. ↩

  3. Steve Blank's customer development writing is a collection of posts, so start with the ones on customer discovery and hypothesis testing. ↩

articles.title: I asked Claude to explain an API request as a tiny machine
articles.description: One prompt with the /anatomy skill gave me an interactive isometric bench for an API request. Here's what each part means, what I changed after the first version, and how to remix it.
articles.body_html:
Hey everyone 👋

Play with it here → mahmad.me/blocks/interactive/api-lifecycle

It started with one line

Anatomy is a Claude skill that explains an idea by building a small machine instead of a diagram. I gave it this:

"/anatomy explain how an API lifecycle works with database and cache, interactive"

The first version already worked: it was a full bench with a shuttle running on a rail. The fun part was the back and forth after that.

Every part means something 🔧

There are no boxes and arrows. Each piece of the machine is a real part of the request:

  • 💳 The card is the request. It rides on a little shuttle with wheels that actually roll.
  • 🚧 The gate is auth. It only lifts when the token is valid.
  • 🗄️ The drawers are the database. A drawer slides out to fetch the row.
  • 💾 The floppy slot on the monitor is where the response lands before it shows on screen.

Click the monitor and it zooms in so you can read the profile.

What I changed after the first version

  • The cache keeps its copy. At first the cache handed its only copy to the shuttle. That's wrong: a cache read doesn't remove anything, so now it makes a copy.
  • No clicking mid-flight. Flushing the cache while a request was on its way caused weird results, so the controls lock until the trip finishes.
  • Realism. I moved the floppy slot to the front of the monitor, gave the shuttle rolling wheels, and made the card slide into the slot in one smooth hop.
  • Zoom controls (+ / − / reset) inside the frame, so you can get close to any station.

Play with it in your favorite AI tool 🤖

Every block on my site has an Open in menu: v0, ChatGPT, Claude or Cursor. It sends the full source along, so you can ask how it works, change it, or build your own machine from it.

Or add it straight to your project:

npx shadcn add https://mahmad.me/r/api-lifecycle.json

Source code

The block and everything else on my site are open source.

If you like it, please give the repo a star ⭐ → github.com/MA-Ahmad/myPortfolio.
It really helps!
