articles.body_html:
Day 26 of 30 Days of Search.

TL;DR

You can build much more than a search interface with Valyu APIs. These ten apps turn retrieved evidence into biomedical research, consulting reports, investment analysis, geopolitical maps, patent discovery, pharmaceutical content reviews, and scientific research briefs. Each profile below includes what the app does, its stack, Valyu's role, a repository link, a live app link, and a screenshot.

One distinction matters: not all ten currently call Search API directly for their main workflow. Some use Search to retrieve evidence for application-owned reasoning. Others use DeepResearch to run a research task and return a cited report. This collection shows both patterns.

What can you build with Valyu Search API and DeepResearch?

A researcher does not need another list of links. They need to compare clinical evidence. A fund manager needs to find the weakness in a thesis. A consultant needs a research brief they can turn into a client discussion.

That is the starting point for these apps: a specific job, with search and research underneath it.

The Valyu Search API returns results your application can reason over. DeepResearch handles a longer investigation and returns research output. The interface, review steps, and next action are where each product becomes different.

App The job it helps with Valyu's role in the current app
Bio Research biomedical questions and life sciences workflows DeepResearch workflows and cited reports
Consult Ralph Prepare company, market, and competitive research DeepResearch with downloadable deliverables
Finance Produce financial research briefs and investment memos DeepResearch workflows and report generation
Global Threat Map Explore geopolitical events and actor intelligence News and entity Search, plus DeepResearch dossiers
Polyseer Investigate a Polymarket or Kalshi market DeepResearch grounded in the market's question and rules
Patents Find patent documents and investigate prior art Search across USPTO and EPO patent sources
OpenWhales Investigate institutional holdings and insider activity SEC and financial Search tools
OpenMLR Pre-check pharmaceutical promotional claims Claim-specific Search, with specialist DeepResearch lanes
Devil's Advocate Challenge an investment thesis against a mandate Sourced research, including DeepResearch for attachment-backed analysis
ARC-AGI-N Discover open research problems and plan an attempt Web and academic Search, plus DeepResearch plans

The screenshots show the hosted interfaces as captured on October 26, 2026. Built-in examples illustrate the products, not independently validated research findings. Some actions require sign-in and credits.

1. Bio: turn a biomedical question into a research brief

Bio helps researchers investigate questions that span scientific papers, clinical trials, drug labels, and patents. Suppose you are comparing approaches to CAR-T treatment for lupus: choose a competitive-landscape workflow, specify the research scope, then review a cited report before deciding which programmes need closer reading. Valyu DeepResearch runs the investigation across biomedical and web sources. Bio adds the life sciences workflow browser, research-depth controls, report history, and deliverables, turning a broad question into material a research team can inspect rather than an unsupported answer.

Stack: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Drizzle, and SQLite or Supabase.

Repository: https://github.com/yorkeccak/bio

Live app: https://bio.valyu.ai

Bio organises research around life sciences jobs. Its output supports research, not clinical diagnosis or treatment decisions.

2. Consult Ralph: start a consulting engagement with a sourced brief

Consult Ralph helps consultants prepare company due diligence, market analysis, competitive intelligence, and industry research. For example, a consultant assessing a market-entry opportunity can name the market, add the client's context and specific questions, and request a brief with supporting files. Valyu DeepResearch performs the research and generates the requested deliverables. The app packages that work into a consulting-specific form and results view, so the next step is reviewing assumptions and shaping a client recommendation, not copying scattered search results into a document.

Stack: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and valyu-js.

Repository: https://github.com/unicodeveloper/consultralph

Live app: https://consultralph.com

The brief starts with the consulting question and client context; the deliverables support the work that follows.

3. Finance: build research around the investment workflow

Finance helps analysts move from a company or investment question to a cited financial research report. An analyst preparing for an investment committee meeting can start with a company profile or memo workflow, set the scope, and inspect the supporting sources before taking a position to the team. The current app uses Valyu DeepResearch and a financial-services workflow catalogue, rather than making the user orchestrate individual searches. Finance provides the report interface, research history, and controls for charts, code execution, and deliverables.

Stack: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Drizzle, and SQLite or Supabase.

Repository: https://github.com/yorkeccak/finance

Live app: https://finance.valyu.ai

Finance turns a financial research question into a reviewable report. It does not execute trades.

4. Global Threat Map: give geopolitical research a geographic interface

Global Threat Map puts security events, geographic context, and actor research on an interactive globe. An analyst investigating a regional disruption can explore the map, narrow the event feed, and investigate a relevant organisation before preparing a briefing. Valyu Search supplies news and entity-background retrieval; DeepResearch supports longer intelligence dossiers. Mapbox handles the geographic interface and map layers. That separation matters: Valyu supplies research evidence, not every flight, fire, or earthquake marker displayed by the app.

Stack: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Mapbox GL JS, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and valyu-js.

Repository: https://github.com/unicodeveloper/globalthreatmap

Live app: https://globalthreatmap.up.railway.app

The captured map is public; its event feed is sign-in gated. A marker is a starting point for investigation, not a verified threat assessment.

5. Polyseer: research the question behind a prediction-market price

Polyseer helps users investigate markets on Polymarket and Kalshi. Paste a market URL, and the app reads the question, prices, closing date, and resolution rules before starting research. Someone examining a central-bank decision market can compare the resulting estimated probability, supporting evidence, and risks against the market price, then decide whether the apparent disagreement deserves more investigation. Valyu DeepResearch runs that investigation and returns structured forecasting output and supporting files. Polyseer supplies the market context and the interface for following the research.

Stack: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and Polymarket/Kalshi API integrations.

Repository: https://github.com/yorkeccak/Polyseer

Live app: https://polyseer.xyz

A research estimate can be wrong. Polyseer is not a guarantee of a forecasting edge or a profitable trade.

6. Patents: move from an invention description to documents worth reading

Patents, branded PatentAI in the interface, helps builders and researchers investigate patent documents in natural language. A hardware team exploring solid-state batteries can describe the mechanism, narrow the jurisdiction, and inspect related patent records and drawings before deciding what to take to a patent professional. Valyu Search retrieves USPTO and EPO patent material; the app adds conversational investigation, patent-identity handling, and analysis tools. The useful outcome is a better set of documents and questions, not an automated declaration that an invention is patentable or safe to commercialise.

Stack: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Vercel AI SDK, valyu-js, Recharts, and Daytona.

Repository: https://github.com/yorkeccak/patents

Live app: https://patents.valyu.ai

Use retrieved patent documents to guide further investigation. Prior-art and freedom-to-operate conclusions require qualified review.

7. OpenWhales: follow institutional and insider disclosures

OpenWhales helps investors investigate what institutions, activist investors, and corporate insiders have disclosed in SEC filings. Search a ticker such as NVDA or an investor's name to explore holdings, transactions, and a sourced narrative, then open the filings behind an interesting change. Valyu's SEC Search tools supply the filing evidence, with additional financial, economic, and company-research tools available for follow-up questions. OpenWhales turns that retrieval into holdings tables, transaction views, and conversational analysis, with Redis caching for repeat requests.

Stack: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Vercel AI SDK, @valyu/ai-sdk, Redis, and Zustand.

Repository: https://github.com/unicodeveloper/openwhales

Live app: https://open-whales.com

A disclosure tells you what was reported for a particular date or period. It is not a live view of an investor's complete portfolio or intentions.

8. OpenMLR: check pharmaceutical claims against retrieved evidence

OpenMLR is a medical, legal, and regulatory pre-check for pharmaceutical promotional content. A reviewer can paste a draft asset containing a comparative efficacy claim, inspect the evidence attached to each finding, and decide whether to accept it, request a revision, or reject it. Valyu Search retrieves claim-specific material from sources such as drug labels, PubMed, and clinical trials, while specialist checks can run through DeepResearch. The app adds claim extraction, review decisions, an audit trail, and a reusable claims library. Human reviewers remain responsible for the determination.

Stack: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, valyu-js, Zod, Streamdown, and optional PostgreSQL.

Repository: https://github.com/unicodeveloper/openmlr

Live app: https://openmlr.up.railway.app

This is the app's preloaded sample, not a review performed for this article or a medical or regulatory endorsement of its findings.

9. Devil's Advocate: challenge an investment thesis before committee

Devil's Advocate helps fund managers stress-test investment memos against evidence and their own mandate. Write a stock, fund, or private-company thesis, then examine objections from bull, bear, and house-view review roles. The next step is addressing the objections or revising the memo before moving it towards investment committee review. Valyu supplies sourced research, including DeepResearch for attachment-backed investigations. The app adds the adversarial review process, per-manager rules, memo states, and PDF export, making the research part of an explicit decision workflow rather than another detached report.

Stack: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Vercel AI SDK, TipTap, Drizzle, SQLite, and Playwright.

Repository: https://github.com/unicodeveloper/devilsadvocate

Live app: https://devilsadvocate.up.railway.app

The screenshot shows read-only examples. An app-level approval is a workflow state, not an investment recommendation.

10. ARC-AGI-N: find a research problem and a place to start

ARC-AGI-N helps people discover open questions in mathematics and science, read the supporting literature, and prepare an agent-ready research brief. Someone interested in climate science can search for problems, inspect the cited sources, choose a tractable starting question, and request a deeper research plan. Valyu Search powers discovery across web and academic material; DeepResearch produces longer plans. The app adds a browsable globe, structured problem cards, and copyable research prompts. It helps choose the next investigation, without claiming to prove that a question remains unsolved.

Stack: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Vercel AI SDK, Mapbox GL JS, valyu-js, and KaTeX.

Repository: https://github.com/yorkeccak/arc-agi-n

Live app: https://arc-agi-n.com

ARC-AGI-N is an independent project, not an official ARC Prize benchmark. Check recent primary literature before claiming a problem is still open.

What these ten apps have in common

The differentiator is not that each app has a search box. It is what happens after retrieval: a document gets reviewed, a thesis gets challenged, a market question gets investigated, or a research problem becomes a concrete next step.

If you are building something similar, start with the user's job and work backwards:

  1. Define the decision or output. A shortlist, research brief, evidence check, or investment memo needs a different interface.
  2. Choose Search or DeepResearch deliberately. Use Search when your application controls retrieval and reasoning. Use DeepResearch when you want a completed investigation and cited output.
  3. Keep the evidence visible. Preserve source links, dates, and relevant passages so someone can check the interpretation.
  4. Make the next action explicit. Open the filing, read the paper, revise the claim, or request a deeper investigation.

You can study the repositories above, check their licences and setup requirements, and adapt the relevant pattern to your own application. For a smaller starting point, see the Valyu quickstart and Vercel AI SDK integration.

Frequently asked questions

Are all ten apps built directly on Valyu Search API?

No. Patents and OpenWhales expose clear application-owned Search patterns. Bio, Finance, Consult Ralph, and Polyseer currently use DeepResearch for their main research workflows. Global Threat Map, OpenMLR, and ARC-AGI-N combine search and longer research. Devil's Advocate uses Valyu research within its memo-review process. Study the current implementation rather than assuming every app follows the same architecture.

Can I run these applications myself?

The repositories are public, and the projects document deployment or local setup. Check each repository's licence, environment variables, required services, and source access before reusing it. Self-hosting the interface does not make API calls free; check current Valyu pricing.

Were the screenshots generated from new paid research runs?

No. They were captured from the hosted interfaces and a public built-in sample review. No new paid research task was launched to prepare this article. Screenshots demonstrate the product interface, not research accuracy, production traffic, or a measured performance benchmark.

Build your next research app

Pick one job from this collection and give your agent the evidence it needs to do it. Start with the API documentation, get a key at platform.valyu.ai, and keep the sources attached to the result.

The search is the beginning. The useful application is what you build around it.

articles.title: All DB access lives in one place
articles.description: One mistake I see in backend codebases:  ORM queries scattered everywhere.  Controllers query the DB....
articles.body_html:
One mistake I see in backend codebases:

ORM queries scattered everywhere.

Controllers query the DB. Services query the DB. Helpers query the DB. The little cron job queries the DB. Change one column and you're grep-ing the whole repo, praying you found every query that touches it.

Soon your database logic is impossible to track — and nobody can tell you where a value actually gets read or written.

A better pattern: the repository layer.

All DB access lives in one place. Controllers ask the repository; they never touch the ORM. Schema knowledge — joins, filters, transaction boundaries — lives in one module per entity. The rest of the codebase just calls methods with names that say what they mean: findActiveUsers(), not db.select().where(...).

Three things this buys you:

  1. Cleaner code — business logic stops drowning in query syntax.
  2. Safer schema changes — rename a column in one file, not seventeen.
  3. A clean test seam — the boundary you need to mock is obvious.

The rule I keep: no raw ORM calls outside the repository. No exceptions for "it's just a small helper." Break the rule once and it's no longer a rule.

All DB access lives in one place. That's the whole point.

Next in this series: debugging a distributed mystery. I write about backend systems that look small until they aren't — follow along if that's your world; the longer pieces live on my Substack.

articles.title: Is Open Source Still Open? A Look at Recent License Changes and Who They Hurt
articles.description: A few years ago, I checked a dependency’s license once, at install time, and never again. That habit...
articles.body_html:
A few years ago, I checked a dependency’s license once, at install time, and never again. That habit is getting expensive.

License changes aren’t new, but they’re happening often enough that “it’s open source” is no longer a permanent property of a project. It’s a status that can change between releases.

The pattern is almost always the same.

The shift nearly always runs one way: from an OSI-approved permissive or copyleft license toward a “source-available” license the Open Source Initiative doesn’t recognize as open source.

The Business Source License (BSL) is the most common destination. It’s a “delayed open source” license: the vendor sets restrictions up front, and each version converts to a true open-source license after a change date, typically four years out.

It’s not just the famous cases anymore. A few from this year alone:

  • Loki Mode moved from the MIT License to BSL 1.1 effective March 19, 2026.
  • Unleash announced in June 2026 that its core repository is moving from Apache 2.0 to AGPLv3. AGPL is OSI-approved, so this one is a different kind of change, but it still affects anyone embedding the code.
  • MiniMax moved its M2.7 AI model from MIT to a non-commercial license, which drew immediate backlash.

Who it actually hurts

  • 1. Small teams and agencies building on top: If your product depends on a library that relicenses, you now have three options: pay, migrate, or fork. Big companies have legal teams for that. A five-person shop usually doesn’t.
  • 2. Contributors: People gave their time to a project under one set of terms. When the company controlling it changes the rules, the community’s work becomes part of a product they no longer fully share in.
  • 3. Downstream projects: Plugins, integrations, and tutorials built around a tool inherit the uncertainty when its license shifts.

The fair counterargument

I don’t think vendors are simply villains here. Many of these changes were a response to cloud providers selling managed versions of a project without funding it. Maintainers need a sustainable model, and “be open and hope for donations” has a poor track record.

It’s also not always one-way. Redis is back under a recognized open-source license for those who choose it, while Valkey continues to be actively developed. Competition between the original and the fork may have pushed both toward better outcomes. Broader data also suggests permissive licensing has been rising, so this isn’t a total collapse of open source.

What I do now

  • Check who controls the project A single company controlling a project can relicense future versions at any time, while a project run by a neutral foundation with many contributing companies is much harder to change.
  • Read the license on every major upgrade, not just at install.
  • Pin versions so a surprise change doesn’t land in your next deploy.
  • Know your exit. Is there a credible fork? A foundation-backed alternative?
  • Set up license-change alerts for your critical dependencies.

So, is open source still open?

My honest answer: the code is still often open. The guarantee isn’t. Open source has always depended on trust, and trust now needs a little due diligence.

Over to you: Has a license change ever forced your team to migrate? Do you think relicensing is a fair business move, or a betrayal of the community that built the project? Tell me in the comments.

articles.title: How EU shops label the 30-day lowest price, and how a browser extension reads them in 15 languages
articles.description: Since 2022 every shop in the EU that advertises a price reduction has to show the lowest price it...
articles.body_html:
Since 2022 every shop in the EU that advertises a price reduction has to show the lowest price it charged in the 30 days before the reduction. That is Article 6a of the Price Indication Directive, added by the Omnibus Directive 2019/2161. The rule is the same everywhere. The way shops print it is not.

I maintain truediscount, a free, open source extension for Chrome and Firefox that puts a small badge on product pages and tells you whether a discount is real. This post is about the messiest part of that job: finding the 30-day price on a page, in whatever language and layout the shop chose.

What the label looks like across countries

A few real phrasings, collected from shop pages:

Country Typical label
Germany, Austria Niedrigster Preis der letzten 30 Tage: 49,99 €
France Prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours : 49,99 €
Italy Prezzo più basso degli ultimi 30 giorni: 49,99 €
Spain Precio más bajo de los últimos 30 días: 49,99 €
Netherlands, Belgium Laagste prijs van de afgelopen 30 dagen: € 49,99
Poland Najniższa cena z 30 dni przed obniżką: 49,99 zł
Czechia Nejnižší cena za posledních 30 dní: 1 299 Kč
Romania Cel mai mic preț din ultimele 30 de zile: 249,99 lei
Sweden Lägsta pris senaste 30 dagarna: 499 kr

On top of the language there are layout differences:

  1. Inline label. The number sits in the same short element as the words. This is the easy case.
  2. Footnote. The struck price carries an asterisk and the explanation lives in the page footer, far away from the number. About You does this with "Letzter niedrigster Preis: der letzten 30 Tage vor der Preisermäßigung".
  3. Tooltip or popover. Alternate puts the explanation in a popover attribute on an info icon next to the price.
  4. Nothing at all next to the struck price. The crossed out number is the shop's own earlier price and you have to trust that it is the 30-day low.
  5. RRP instead. The struck price is the manufacturer's recommended price ("UVP" in German, "PVPR" in Spanish, "adviesprijs" in Dutch). Comparing against RRP is legal, but it says nothing about what the shop charged last month.

Case 5 matters most for shoppers, because "was 599, now 349" reads like a 42% cut when it is really a cut against a list price nobody paid.

How the extension reads it

The extractor runs in three passes, all on the page that is already open. Nothing is crawled and nothing leaves the browser.

Pass 1: the current price. Structured data first (JSON-LD Product and Offer, including products nested inside other types, then microdata), then a per shop selector if one exists, then generic selectors.

Pass 2: the advertised old price. Per shop selectors first, then generic ones such as s, del, [style*="line-through"] and class names containing old-price or strike. A candidate only counts if it is higher than the current price and less than 20 times it, which filters out unrelated numbers.

The kind of old price is decided by its label. The newest fix (v0.9.0) came from Lidl, which renders UVP: <s>599.00</s>. The word sits in the parent element, not inside the <s>, so the extension now also looks at the short parent text:

const label = (el.parentElement?.textContent || '').length < 60 ? el.parentElement.textContent : '';
oldKind = /rrp|uvp|retail price|adviesprijs|\bmsrp\b/i.test(`${selector} ${el.textContent} ${label} ${hint}`)
  ? 'rrp' : 'previous';

On lidl.fr the same layout shows a bare <s>49.99 €</s> with no label, and that stays a "previous price".

Pass 3: the shop's own 30-day disclosure. Two regular expressions do most of the work (shortened here): one for "lowest" in about 15 languages and one for "30 days":

const LOW_WORD = /(lowest|niedrigste|tiefstpreis|le plus bas|più basso|más bajo|laagste|najniższa|nejnižší|cel mai mic|lägsta|laveste|alhaisin|legalacsonyabb|najniža)/iu;
const DAYS_30 = /30[\s\u00a0-]*(?:tage?n?|days?|jours|giorni|días|dagen|dagarna|dni|dní|zile|dana|nap)/giu;

When both match inside a short element, the first price in that element becomes the shop's declared 30-day low. Prices are parsed with EU formats in mind: 1.299,99 €, 1 299 Kč, 49,- and € 49,99 all come out as numbers.

The verdict

With those three numbers the badge says one of a few things:

  • The old price matches the shop's 30-day low: the discount is real.
  • The old price is higher than the declared 30-day low: the discount is inflated, and the badge shows the real percentage.
  • The old price is an RRP: the badge says so and shows the 30-day low if the shop printed one.
  • No disclosure on the page: the extension falls back to its own local price history (one price per day, kept 90 days on your device).

What is still hard

  • Footnote layouts (case 2) are only understood when the footnote is close to the price. Matching asterisks across a whole page gives too many false hits.
  • Many shops render prices with JavaScript after load, so the content script watches the page for changes and checks again once it settles.
  • Several big shops block automated requests, so I can only build per shop rules from pages I can actually load. The supported shops page says which shops are tested against live pages and which only use generic rules.

If a shop near you prints the 30-day label in a way the extension misses, the popup has a "Report a problem" button that opens a prefilled GitHub issue with just the domain. That is the fastest way to get a new country covered before Black Friday. And if the badge gets in the way on a site you do not care about, v0.10.0 lets you hide it per domain from the popup; nothing is recorded on hidden sites.

Code and builds: github.com/emirmrkaljevic/truediscount

This article was written with AI assistance.

articles.title: Python 3.14's concurrent.interpreters module turns a 3.6-second GIL bottleneck into 0.9 seconds
articles.description: I measured Python 3.14's new subinterpreters against threads and processes: 3.6s of GIL contention dropped to 0.9s, but a single interpreter flatly refuses a second concurrent thread.
articles.body_html:
A CPU-bound Python job split across four threads took 3.6 seconds on my machine. The same job split across four of Python 3.14's new subinterpreters took 0.9 seconds, roughly what one thread alone takes to do a quarter of the work. That part matched what I expected from the PEP. What I did not expect was that asking one of those subinterpreters to run two things at once does not slow it down. It refuses outright.

concurrent.interpreters is new in the standard library as of Python 3.14, released on 7 October 2026. Subinterpreters themselves are not new - they have existed in the C API since Python 1.5 and CPython has used them internally for years - but PEP 734 is what makes them usable from ordinary Python code, with no C extension required. Each subinterpreter gets its own Global Interpreter Lock, which is the part worth testing: it is the thing that is supposed to let CPU-bound Python code actually use more than one core without reaching for multiprocessing.

I tested it against a CPU-bound workload (counting primes below 400,000, a plain Python double loop with no C extensions to hide behind), compared against threads, processes, and a single thread, three runs each, inside a python:3.14-slim container with four cores available.

The headline number

approach time for 4x the work
single thread (1x unit, for reference) 0.77 - 0.80s
4 OS threads, classic GIL 3.51 - 3.70s
4 subinterpreters (new in 3.14) 0.89 - 0.98s
4 processes (multiprocessing) 0.95 - 1.30s

Four threads doing four units of CPU-bound work took more than four times as long as one thread doing one unit - 3.6s against roughly 0.8s, which is actually a bit worse than the 3.2s you'd get from perfect serialisation, because the GIL has to keep stopping one thread to let another run. Four subinterpreters doing the same four units took about 0.9s: close enough to the single-unit baseline that the extra three units of work were, for practical purposes, free. That is real parallelism, not a scheduling trick, and it lands in the same place multiprocessing already does.

What it refuses: one thread per interpreter, not shared

The PEP's selling point is that each interpreter has its own GIL. I wanted to see what happens when two threads try to use one interpreter's GIL at the same time, expecting it to behave like classic Python: both threads run, the shared GIL makes them take turns.

That is not what happened. A single Interpreter object only tolerates one caller. A second concurrent call doesn't queue, and it doesn't share time with the first - it is rejected immediately:

Exception in thread Thread-2 (_call):
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.14/concurrent/interpreters/__init__.py", line 226, in _call
    res, excinfo = _interpreters.call(self._id, callable, args, kwargs, restrict=True)
concurrent.interpreters.InterpreterError: interpreter already running

I confirmed the shape of this with three variants of the same interpreter, run in sequence:

scenario time outcome
one call 0.84s fine
two sequential calls, same interpreter 1.63s fine, roughly 2x
two concurrent calls, same interpreter 0.84s wall-clock second call raises InterpreterError

interpreters.create() is documented as returning "a new (idle) Python interpreter", and that word is accurate: idle or running, nothing in between. If you want N things running at once, you need N interpreters, one each. A thread pool aimed at a single shared interpreter - the pattern every ThreadPoolExecutor tutorial uses with regular threads - does not translate. You get one interpreter's worth of work and an exception, not graceful serialisation.

The opposite number: interpreters are not obviously cheaper to start than processes

The other assumption I walked in with was that subinterpreters, being lighter than OS processes, would be cheap to spin up. I measured the cost of creating four workers and giving each one some real state (a 200,000-element list), steady state after the first warm-up run:

approach create + populate, 4 workers
fork (Python 3.13's Linux default) 0.037 - 0.038s
forkserver (Python 3.14's Linux default) 0.057 - 0.065s
4 subinterpreters 0.076 - 0.078s

Creating four subinterpreters and running a small amount of code in each took about twice as long as a classic fork-based process pool, and somewhat longer than the new forkserver default too. None of this matters once the work inside each worker takes more than a few milliseconds - the 3.6s-versus-0.9s number above swallows an 80-millisecond setup cost without noticing. But it means "subinterpreters are lighter than processes" is not something I could verify at creation time; the saving, where it exists, is in not forking a second copy of the process's address space, not in any faster start.

That forkserver row was an accident. I wrote a timing script that called multiprocessing.Process(...).start() directly from the module's top level, the way plenty of tutorial code still does, and it crashed:

RuntimeError:
        An attempt has been made to start a new process before the
        current process has finished its bootstrapping phase.

Checking multiprocessing.get_start_method() explained it: Python 3.14 changed the default start method on Linux from fork to forkserver. Python 3.13 reports fork; 3.14 reports forkserver. forkserver re-imports your module in the child, which is exactly the thing if __name__ == "__main__": exists to guard against, and which fork never required you to bother with. Every piece of multiprocessing code I'd written without that guard over the years happened to work by accident, on Linux, until this release. It's a one-line fix, but it is a real break, and it landed in the same release that gives you an alternative that doesn't have this problem at all.

What it costs: closing an interpreter doesn't give the memory back

I ran four rounds of "create four interpreters, give each a 200,000-element list, close them", watching my own process's RSS the whole time:

round 1: 16920 -> 55648 KB
round 2: 55648 -> 57140 KB
round 3: 57140 -> 59476 KB
round 4: 59476 -> 61096 KB

.close() does finalise the interpreter - a destroyed interpreter can't be called again, and I checked that it raises if you try - but the process's resident memory never drops back to where it started. It flattens out (each later round adds less than the first) rather than growing without bound, which looks like CPython's allocator holding onto freed arenas rather than a genuine leak, but I didn't chase that further. If you're planning to cycle through many short-lived interpreters inside one long-running process, budget for that memory to stay resident, not to be returned to the OS the way a finished process's memory is.

What's actually shareable between interpreters

Subinterpreters don't share objects by default - that is the entire point, it's what lets them skip the GIL - so most interesting values need to cross a boundary. is_shareable() gives a yes/no answer per type:

int              -> True
str              -> True
bytes            -> True
None             -> True
bool             -> True
tuple of ints    -> True
float            -> True
list             -> False
dict             -> False

Passing a threading.Lock as an argument to Interpreter.call() fails immediately, with the repr of the offending object right there in the message:

NotShareableError: (<unlocked _thread.lock object at 0x7f61b8b5add0>,) does not support cross-interpreter data

An ordinary custom class instance fails the same way, with a flatter message:

NotShareableError: object does not support cross-interpreter data

But the cross-interpreter Queue that the same module provides does not enforce this. I put a plain custom-class instance onto a queue and it went through without complaint, and came back out as a distinct, working object with the same attribute values - the queue silently pickles and unpickles it:

q = interpreters.create_queue()
q.put(Thing())          # no error
received = q.get()
# received is not the original object, but received.value is unchanged

So "not shareable" is enforced differently depending on how the object crosses over. A direct argument to call() is checked against the strict shareable-types list and rejected on the spot. The same object dropped into a Queue gets the softer treatment the docs describe for put(): pickled going in, unpickled coming out as a new, unrelated object. If your code passes data between interpreters by argument, moving it to a queue instead buys you a much larger set of types - at the cost of identity and, for anything mutable, of staying in sync with the original.

What I got wrong on the way

My first attempt at the shareability tests put several checks in one script with no if __name__ == "__main__": guard, calling interp.call() with a mix of shareable and non-shareable arguments one after another. Running it printed every result twice, and the second copy sometimes disagreed with the first about which error got raised. My best explanation, which I didn't fully verify, is that call()'s documented pickle fallback needs to resolve names against the target interpreter's own __main__, and since that interpreter had never run my module, resolving anything defined at module level meant running the whole module there first - silently re-executing my test file a second time, inside the subinterpreter, with its own fresh state. Splitting each check into its own small script with a proper __main__ guard made every result reproducible, which is what's reported above. I'd treat any subinterpreter test that imports a lot of top-level code as suspect until it survives being run twice.

Run it yourself

This needs Python 3.14 and four-ish cores to see the gap clearly. I ran it in Docker because that's the fastest way to get an exact version:

docker pull python:3.14-slim

The core benchmark:

# bench.py
import time, threading, sys

def cpu_work(n):
    count = 0
    for i in range(2, n):
        is_prime = True
        for d in range(2, int(i ** 0.5) + 1):
            if i % d == 0:
                is_prime = False
                break
        if is_prime:
            count += 1
    return count

def run_threads(n, workers):
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=cpu_work, args=(n,)) for _ in range(workers)]
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()
    print(f"threads={workers}: {time.perf_counter()-t0:.3f}s")

def run_interpreters(n, workers):
    import concurrent.interpreters as interpreters
    interps = [interpreters.create() for _ in range(workers)]
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    threads = [i.call_in_thread(cpu_work, n) for i in interps]
    for t in threads: t.join()
    print(f"interpreters={workers}: {time.perf_counter()-t0:.3f}s")
    for i in interps: i.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mode, n, workers = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), int(sys.argv[3])
    {"threads": run_threads, "interpreters": run_interpreters}[mode](n, workers)

docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w python:3.14-slim python3 bench.py threads 400000 4
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w python:3.14-slim python3 bench.py interpreters 400000 4

And the refusal, which needs no setup at all:

docker run --rm python:3.14-slim python3 -c "
import concurrent.interpreters as interpreters
i = interpreters.create()
t1 = i.call_in_thread(lambda: __import__('time').sleep(1))
t2 = i.call_in_thread(lambda: __import__('time').sleep(1))
t1.join(); t2.join()
"

What to do with this

If you have a CPU-bound Python workload that multiprocessing already parallelises well, subinterpreters aren't an obvious upgrade yet: on this release they start up slower than a plain fork and about the same as forkserver, and you still need one interpreter per concurrent task, with no pooling against a single interpreter. Where they're worth trying now is the code that currently reaches for a thread, because threading is simpler to wire up than multiprocessing, and then quietly gets nothing from the GIL: swap the Thread for an Interpreter.call_in_thread, and check your data either fits the shareable-types list or is willing to cross as a pickled copy through a Queue. And if you have multiprocessing code anywhere that starts a Process without an if __name__ == "__main__": guard, fix that first - 3.14 will find it on Linux even if nothing else in this post applies to you.

articles.title: How I finally understood the Liskov Substitution Principle
articles.description: The Intro   Halfway through SOLID! We are at the L, the one with the scary name: the Liskov...
articles.body_html:
The Intro

Halfway through SOLID! We are at the L, the one with the scary name: the Liskov Substitution Principle.

If the previous two felt like common sense with fancy labels, this one is the first that usually catches people off guard. I have shipped the exact bug we are about to write. More than once. 🙃

The What

The original definition is a math paper from 1987 and reads like one:

If S is a subtype of T, then objects of type T may be replaced with objects of type S without altering any of the desirable properties of the program.

Let me translate: if your code works with the parent, it must also work with any child, without surprises. No instanceof checks, no "oh but not that one".

The usual example is squares and rectangles. I have never once had a square in production, so let's do something you will actually run into: payments and refunds.

The How

Our store accepts a few ways to pay. Each one can charge and refund:

// src/payment-method.ts
export abstract class PaymentMethod {
  abstract charge(amount: number): Promise<void>
  abstract refund(amount: number): Promise<void>
}

// src/card-payment.ts
import { PaymentMethod } from './payment-method.js'

export class CardPayment extends PaymentMethod {
  async charge(amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 charged $${amount}`)
  }

  async refund(amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 refunded $${amount}`)
  }
}

// src/paypal-payment.ts
import { PaymentMethod } from './payment-method.js'

export class PaypalPayment extends PaymentMethod {
  async charge(amount: number) {
    console.log(`🅿️ charged $${amount}`)
  }

  async refund(amount: number) {
    console.log(`🅿️ refunded $${amount}`)
  }
}

And the part that uses them never cares which one it got:

// src/refund-service.ts
import type { PaymentMethod } from './payment-method.js'

interface Order {
  id: string
  total: number
  paidWith: PaymentMethod
}

export class RefundService {
  async refundAll(orders: Order[]) {
    for (const order of orders) {
      await order.paidWith.refund(order.total)
      console.log(`✅ order ${order.id} refunded`)
    }
  }
}

Beautiful. Substitutable. Barbara Liskov would be proud.

Then product adds gift cards. Gift cards can be charged, obviously. But legal says gift cards can't be refunded to cash. So we write the "obvious" thing:

// src/gift-card-payment.ts
import { PaymentMethod } from './payment-method.js'

export class GiftCardPayment extends PaymentMethod {
  async charge(amount: number) {
    console.log(`🎁 charged $${amount}`)
  }

  async refund() {
    throw new Error('Gift cards cannot be refunded')
  }
}

It compiles. TypeScript is happy. The PR gets approved. 🚢

Three weeks later a product gets recalled and support runs the "refund everyone who bought it" script:

// src/main.ts
import { RefundService } from './refund-service.js'
import { CardPayment } from './card-payment.js'
import { GiftCardPayment } from './gift-card-payment.js'

const orders = [
  { id: 'A1', total: 40, paidWith: new CardPayment() },
  { id: 'A2', total: 25, paidWith: new GiftCardPayment() },
  { id: 'A3', total: 60, paidWith: new CardPayment() },
]

await new RefundService().refundAll(orders)

Output:

💳 refunded $40
✅ order A1 refunded
Error: Gift cards cannot be refunded

Order A1 refunded. Order A2 blew up. Order A3? Never happened. Customer A3 is now writing a one-star review.

That's a Liskov violation. RefundService was written against PaymentMethod, and the contract of PaymentMethod says "I can refund". GiftCardPayment said it was a PaymentMethod and then broke the promise at runtime.

The usual "fix" makes it worse:

if (order.paidWith instanceof GiftCardPayment) continue

Now RefundService knows about gift cards. Tomorrow it has to know about store credit. Then crypto. The whole point of the base class was to not know.

Step 1: stop lying in the type

The real problem is that the parent promised something not every child can keep. So let's make the promise smaller:

// src/payment-method.ts
export interface PaymentMethod {
  charge(amount: number): Promise<void>
}

export interface Refundable {
  refund(amount: number): Promise<void>
}

(Yes, we swapped the abstract class for interfaces. There was no shared code in the base anyway.)

Step 2: each method tells the truth 

// src/card-payment.ts
import type { PaymentMethod, Refundable } from './payment-method.js'

export class CardPayment implements PaymentMethod, Refundable {
  async charge(amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 charged $${amount}`)
  }

  async refund(amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 refunded $${amount}`)
  }
}

// src/gift-card-payment.ts
import type { PaymentMethod } from './payment-method.js'

export class GiftCardPayment implements PaymentMethod {
  async charge(amount: number) {
    console.log(`🎁 charged $${amount}`)
  }
}

No refund() on the gift card. No throw. It just doesn't claim to be something it isn't.

Step 3: ask for exactly what you need 

// src/refund-service.ts
import type { Refundable } from './payment-method.js'

interface RefundableOrder {
  id: string
  total: number
  paidWith: Refundable
}

export class RefundService {
  async refundAll(orders: RefundableOrder[]) {
    for (const order of orders) {
      await order.paidWith.refund(order.total)
      console.log(`✅ order ${order.id} refunded`)
    }
  }
}

And now the best part. Go back to main.ts and try to pass a gift card order into refundAll():

Type 'GiftCardPayment' is not assignable to type 'Refundable'.
  Property 'refund' is missing in type 'GiftCardPayment'.

The compiler caught it. At build time. Not at 2 PM on recall day.

Whoever writes the refund script now has to decide up front what to do with gift card orders (issue store credit, email the customer, whatever). The decision moved from "a crash in a loop" to "a red squiggle in the editor".

The Why

Let's be explicit about the lesson, because it is subtle:

  • Inheritance is a promise, not a shortcut. "GiftCard is a PaymentMethod" sounded right in English. In code, it meant "GiftCard can do everything PaymentMethod can do", and that was false.
  • A method that throws NotSupported is a red flag. If a child has to disable a parent's method, the parent's contract is too big. Shrink it.
  • Callers depend on the smallest thing they need. RefundService needs refunds, so it asks for Refundable. Not PaymentMethod. Not CardPayment.
  • The type system becomes your QA. Every wrong combination fails to compile instead of failing in production.

If you remember one sentence: a subclass may do more than its parent, never less.

The Goodbye

Did you notice that fixing the L made us split one fat interface into two thin ones? That's not a coincidence. That's the I (Interface Segregation) knocking on the door, and it's up next.

Go search your codebase for throw new Error('not supported'). I'll wait. Happy coding 🤝

articles.title: Your secrets don't need a git commit to leak into an AI tool
articles.description: Most of us have the "don't commit secrets" reflex drilled in. Pre-commit hooks, secret scanners in...
articles.body_html:
Most of us have the "don't commit secrets" reflex drilled in. Pre-commit hooks, secret scanners in CI, .env in .gitignore. Good. That covers the repo.

It doesn't cover the context window.

The gap: the repo is not the boundary anymore

When you work with an AI coding assistant, what leaves your machine isn't just the file you're editing. It's whatever you paste, whatever the extension decides is relevant, and whatever the agent reads while it's "helping." The security boundary now includes the editor extension, the chat history, any telemetry, and every service that processes that context on the way to the model and back.

Secret scanners watch commits. Nothing in a typical setup watches what you paste into a chat panel at 6pm while a deploy is failing.

Here are the usual ways a secret ends up in context without ever touching git.

1. The failing test that prints its config

An integration test fails. The assertion message helpfully dumps the client object, which includes the connection string with the password inline. You copy the whole test output into the assistant and ask "why is this failing?"

The question was about the assertion. The payload included the credential.

2. The environment dump 

$ env | sort
...
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:...@db.internal:5432/prod
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_...

"Here's my environment, why can't the app find the config?" is a completely normal debugging move. It's also the fastest way to hand over every key on the box in one paste. Agents that can run shell commands can do this on their own if you let them.

3. Logs that log too much

A verbose HTTP client logs request headers. One of them is Authorization: Bearer .... You paste 200 lines of log to get help with a timeout, and line 143 is a live token.

4. The copied snippet

Someone shares a "working example" in Slack with the key still in it. You paste it into the assistant to adapt it. Now it's in two systems you don't control instead of one.

(These are illustrative scenarios, not specific incidents, but if you've debugged anything under pressure you've probably seen at least one.)

What actually helps

  • Minimize what you send. Paste the relevant ten lines, not the whole log. Ask about the error, not the environment.
  • Redact before pasting. Mask tokens, connection strings and headers. A small shell function or editor snippet that scrubs obvious patterns is worth having.
  • Scope your credentials. If a dev key does leak, it should only be able to touch dev. Short-lived, least-privilege keys shrink the blast radius.
  • Check how your tool handles data. What's retained, for how long, whether it's used for training, what the extension sends automatically, where telemetry goes. These are often separate settings and separate policies. One "privacy" toggle rarely answers all of them.
  • Restrict what agents can read. If your assistant can open files and run commands, keep .env, credential files and secret stores out of its reach.

If it already happened

Deleting the chat message is not remediation. You don't know what was logged, cached or forwarded before you hit delete. Treat it like any other exposure: rotate the credential, revoke the old one, check access logs for use.

The reframe

Secret management used to be a version control problem. With AI tools in the loop, it's a data-flow problem: anything that reaches the model's context has, to some degree, left your control.

The safest secret is the one that never enters the context in the first place.

How does your team handle this today? Do you have any tooling that checks what goes into an AI assistant, or is it all down to developer habit?
