articles.body_html:
1. Introduction

When developing an application or service, one of the common questions we face is how many concurrent requests it can handle and how the services it depends on will respond. Even if we verify that all functionalities work correctly, this does not guarantee that the system will maintain its performance as demand increases.

This is why software testing goes beyond verifying functional requirements. It also allows us to evaluate aspects such as performance, stability, and responsiveness. In particular, load testing is not simply about pushing a system until it fails, but rather about understanding how it behaves under different conditions and identifying when it stops meeting the expected requirements.

In the previous article, we built a service to identify duplicate products using Amazon Bedrock, S3 Vectors, and DynamoDB, including an AWS Lambda function to perform real-time searches. During our initial tests, the service responded within a few seconds, but one question remained unanswered: how would it behave if many users accessed it simultaneously?

To answer this question, in this second part, we will expose the service through Amazon API Gateway and evaluate its behavior under load. Before running the tests, however, we need to define what we want to measure and which criteria we will use to evaluate the results. To do this, we will introduce some fundamental concepts of Site Reliability Engineering (SRE). We will then automate load testing with Grafana k6 on AWS and, finally, generate a report in which generative AI will help us interpret the collected metrics.

2. Understanding Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)

2.1. What Is SRE?

Before evaluating how our API behaves under load, we need to establish what acceptable performance and reliability actually mean. A service may continue responding to requests, but that does not necessarily mean it is meeting the expected performance requirements.

This is where Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) comes into play. Originally developed at Google, SRE is a discipline that applies software engineering principles to operating and maintaining reliable systems. It focuses on defining measurable objectives, selecting indicators that reflect service behavior, and using automation to reduce repetitive operational tasks.
For our use case, these concepts provide a foundation for moving beyond simply checking whether the API responds. Instead, we can evaluate specific indicators such as response times, error rates, and performance under different load conditions.

2.2. Seven Principles of SRE

SRE is built on a set of principles that guide how reliable services are designed, operated, and maintained. These range from defining reliability objectives and managing risk to automation, monitoring, and keeping systems as simple as possible.
The following infographic summarizes seven of these principles, based on Google's Site Reliability Engineering book.


Illustration by the author. Based on Google's Site Reliability Engineering book.

2.3. Capacity Planning and Performance

Service reliability depends not only on availability but also on the ability to handle demand while maintaining acceptable performance. In this context, SRE includes several practices aimed at anticipating problems, optimizing resources, and reducing the impact of changes in production.

Among these practices, we can highlight:

  • Capacity Planning: ensuring that a system has sufficient resources and redundancy to handle expected demand without compromising availability objectives. To support this, Google recommends regular load testing to assess the actual capacity of a service.
  • Efficiency and Performance: understanding how performance changes as load increases, identifying potential degradation, and finding opportunities to optimize resource utilization.
  • Change Management: reducing the risks associated with changes in production. According to Google's documented experience, approximately 70% of service outages are caused by changes to live systems, highlighting the importance of detecting problems early. These practices are directly related to our use case, as we aim to evaluate our API's performance under different load conditions.

2.4. SLI, SLO, and SLA

Evaluating a service's capacity and performance requires more than simply running tests and collecting metrics. We also need to define what we want to measure and which service levels we consider acceptable.

In this context, SRE introduces three related concepts: SLI (Service Level Indicator), SLO (Service Level Objective), and SLA (Service Level Agreement). Together, they connect technical measurements with service objectives and commitments.

The following infographic summarizes what each concept represents, the question it helps answer, and a practical example of how it can be applied.


Illustration by the author. Based on Google's SRE framework.

3. Grafana k6: A Tool for Performance Testing

Grafana k6 is an open-source tool developed in Go and maintained by Grafana Labs, designed to perform load and performance testing on applications, APIs, and microservices. Test scenarios are defined using JavaScript, making it easier to automate tests and integrate them into development workflows.

Although we often associate these tools with stress testing, k6 allows us to evaluate how a system behaves under different load conditions, without necessarily pushing it to the point of failure.


Illustration by the author. Based on Grafana k6 documentation.

3.1. Types of Load Tests

Depending on what we want to evaluate, we can define different test scenarios:

  • Smoke: verify that the system responds correctly under minimal load.
  • Average-load: evaluate system behavior under normal operating conditions.
  • Stress: assess how the system responds under high load.
  • Soak: identify potential performance degradation when load is sustained over extended periods.
  • Spike: evaluate how the system responds to sudden increases in traffic.
  • Breakpoint: progressively increase the load to identify the point at which the system stops meeting the expected criteria. These scenarios allow us to analyze different aspects of system performance. We should also consider that an application often depends on multiple components and services, meaning that performance degradation can originate from different parts of its architecture.

3.2. Main Components of k6

To execute these tests, k6 provides several components that allow us to configure load, validate responses, collect metrics, and integrate results with other tools.


Illustration by the author. Based on Grafana k6 documentation.

We can group them into four main components:

  • ⚙️ Options: define how a test will be executed. They allow us to configure scenarios, load stages, virtual users (VUs), duration, iterations, and acceptance thresholds. These options enable us to reproduce the different types of tests described earlier.
  • ✅ Checks: validate conditions on received responses, such as HTTP status codes or response content. A failed check is recorded in the metrics but does not automatically stop the test execution.
  • 📊 Metrics: collect information about system behavior, including response times, request counts, and error rates. k6 provides built-in metrics and supports custom metrics.
  • 🔗 Integrations: allow tests to be incorporated into CI/CD pipelines and results to be exported to storage, monitoring, and visualization tools. In our case, we will use CSV and JSON to store the results and subsequently process the metrics included in the final report.

4. Architecture

Our load testing solution builds on the game-catalog-resolve-product Lambda function developed in the previous article, which uses Amazon Bedrock, S3 Vectors, and DynamoDB to identify duplicate products.

In this second part, we expose the function through Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) with IAM authorization, requiring k6 requests to be signed using AWS credentials.

The testing process is automated using AWS Step Functions, which orchestrates k6 execution on Amazon ECS Fargate and subsequent report generation through an AWS Lambda function. Test scripts and results are stored in Amazon S3, while Amazon ECR stores the container images.

The entire infrastructure is defined using Terraform, and the code is available on GitHub, making the solution reproducible.


Architecture diagram by the author.

5. Use Case: Automated Load Testing

In this use case, we will run different load testing scenarios against our API. To do this, we use Grafana k6 running inside a Docker container to send requests and collect performance metrics. Once the tests are complete, a Python-based process calculates the results and generates a PDF report that includes an interpretation provided by Amazon Bedrock.


Illustration by the author.

5.1. The Repository

The project is available on GitHub: game-catalog-k6.

RominaElenaMendezEscobar / game-catalog-k6

Load testing a GenAI API on AWS with k6: scenarios defined in JSON (smoke, load, stress, spike) run on ECS Fargate and orchestrated by Step Functions. Metrics from k6 and CloudWatch are collected by Lambda, and Amazon Bedrock generates an analysis of the results. Tests an API Gateway endpoint backed by Lambda, Amazon Bedrock and S3 Vectors.

⚡ Automated API Load Testing on AWS: Grafana k6 and AI-Powered Reporting with Amazon Bedrock

Serverless pipeline that runs Grafana k6 load tests against an API on Amazon ECS Fargate orchestrated by AWS Step Functions, and generates a PDF report where Amazon Bedrock interprets the metrics. All the infrastructure is defined with Terraform.

📝 Article: 🔗 Part 1 (the API under test): Identical or Similar? AI-Powered Product Matching with Amazon Bedrock and S3 Vectors · repository

🎯 What it does

  1. Runs a load test with k6 in a container on ECS Fargate, using a configurable scenario (smoke, load, stress, spike).
  2. Stores every run in its own S3 folder, with the results and an exact copy of the scenario used.
  3. Generates a PDF report: metrics are computed by code; Amazon Bedrock only interprets them, and the figures it quotes are validated against the computed metrics.

The thresholds…

View on GitHub

Its structure includes the k6 scripts, test scenarios, report generator, and infrastructure defined using Terraform.
game-catalog-k6/
├── Dockerfile, entrypoint.sh
├── search.js, sigv4.js
├── scenarios/
├── queries.json
├── report/
│   └── config/
├── terraform/
└── build-and-push.sh

The goal is to make this solution reusable for testing other APIs without modifying the underlying infrastructure or the report generation process. To do this, we only need to configure three elements:

  • 〰️ The API we want to test
  • 〰️ The requests we want to send
  • 〰️ The load testing scenarios

5.2. Configuring Tests for Another API

1. Identify the API: api_id

In our case, we use Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) with IAM authorization. The service URL follows this structure:

https://<api-id>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com

The API identifier can be found in the AWS Management Console under API Gateway → Your API → API details.
To configure the project, we specify it in terraform/terraform.tfvars:

api_id = "<api-id>"

Terraform uses this identifier to construct the API URL and configure the necessary permissions for the k6 container to invoke the API using IAM-signed requests.

2. Define the Requests: queries.json

Once we have identified the API, we need to define which requests we want to send.
Our API accepts text searches through POST /search. To define the requests executed during testing, we use the queries.json file, which contains different video game searches in English and Spanish.

[
  {"query": "fifa 14 ps3 digital code", "lang": "en"},
  {"query": "fifa 14 ps3 codigo digital", "lang": "es"},
  {"query": "gta vice city ps2", "lang": "en"},
  {"query": "el mario kart de la wii", "lang": "es"}
]

If the API expects a different request structure, we will also need to adapt the request body in search.js.

3. Configure the Load: scenarios

Once we have defined what to request, we need to establish how the load will be applied. For this, we use JSON files in the scenarios/ directory, each with its own configuration.

Each JSON file defines a different load testing scenario:

  • smoke.json — Smoke Test: 1 virtual user for 1 minute to verify basic functionality.
  • load.json — Load Test: 5 virtual users for 5 minutes to evaluate system behavior under steady load.
  • stress.json — Stress Test: gradually increases the load from 5 to 40 virtual users over 6 minutes to identify performance degradation.
  • spike.json — Spike Test: increases the load from 0 to 50 virtual users in 30 seconds to evaluate how the system responds to sudden traffic spikes. Each scenario can be customized by adjusting the number of virtual users, test duration, load pattern, and performance thresholds.

Each file allows us to configure virtual users, test duration, load patterns, and performance thresholds.
For example, smoke.json contains:

{
  "name": "smoke",
  "description": "1 user for 1 minute: checks that the API works before adding load.",
  "queries_file": "queries.json",
  "endpoint": "/search",
  "think_time_seconds": 1,
  "executor": {
    "executor": "constant-vus",
    "vus": 1,
    "duration": "1m"
  },
  "thresholds": {
    "http_req_failed": ["rate<0.01"],
    "http_req_duration": ["p(95)<5000"]
  }
}

The main parameters are:

  • endpoint: the API path to which requests will be sent.
  • think_time_seconds: the pause between requests made by each virtual user.
  • executor: defines the load pattern, number of virtual users, and test duration.
  • thresholds: allows us to define acceptance criteria for the metrics. In this example, an error rate below 1% and a p95 response time below 5 seconds. These thresholds allow us to translate our performance objectives into measurable acceptance criteria during testing, following the SLI and SLO concepts introduced earlier. We can modify existing scenarios or create new JSON files to evaluate different load conditions while reusing the same k6 code.

5.3. Deploying the Infrastructure with Terraform

Once the configuration files are ready, we can deploy the solution using AWS CloudShell, with the tools needed to run Terraform and build Docker images.

1. Install Terraform (First Time Only)

AWS CloudShell does not include Terraform by default. We can download it to our home directory, which persists across sessions:

curl -sLo /tmp/terraform.zip https://releases.hashicorp.com/terraform/1.9.8/terraform_1.9.8_linux_amd64.zip
mkdir -p ~/bin && unzip -o /tmp/terraform.zip -d ~/bin
echo 'export PATH="HOME/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc && source ~/.bashrc
terraform version

2. Create the Infrastructure 

git clone https://github.com/RominaElenaMendezEscobar/game-catalog-k6.git
cd game-catalog-k6/terraform
echo 'api_id = "<api-id>"' > terraform.tfvars
terraform init
terraform apply \
  -target=aws_ecr_repository.k6 \
  -target=aws_ecr_repository.report
../build-and-push.sh

terraform apply

The deployment is performed in three stages: first, we create the Amazon ECR repositories; next, we build and push the container images; and finally, we deploy the remaining resources.

Terraform provisions the required infrastructure, including Amazon ECS Fargate, AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, Amazon S3, and IAM roles and permissions. It also uploads the test scenarios and queries that k6 will use to Amazon S3.

5.4. Running a Load Test

With the infrastructure deployed, we can start a test execution using AWS Step Functions, specifying the scenario we want to run.
For example, to execute load.json:

aws stepfunctions start-execution \
  --state-machine-arn "$(terraform output -raw state_machine_arn)" \
  --input '{"scenario": "load", "label": "baseline"}'


Screenshot by the author. AWS Management Console.

The state machine orchestrates three steps:

  • PrepareRun: takes the scenario and label provided in the input and generates a unique identifier based on the date and time (run_id). This identifier is used in the following two steps to ensure that the results and report are associated with the same test execution.
  • RunLoadTest: starts the k6 container on Amazon ECS Fargate, executes the selected scenario, and stores the results in Amazon S3.
  • GenerateReport: processes the results using an AWS Lambda function, calculates the metrics, and generates a PDF report with an interpretation provided by Amazon Bedrock. Each execution is stored in a separate folder, following a structure such as runs/<scenario>/<date>/, along with the configuration used for the test.


Screenshot by the author. Amazon S3 bucket showing the files and results generated by the automated load testing pipeline.

Generated by k6 (RunLoadTest):

  • k6-summary.json: a summary of the test, including aggregated metric values (averages, percentiles, error rates) and threshold evaluation results.
  • k6-results.csv: detailed data for each request, including when it was sent, how long it took, and whether it failed. This data is used to generate time-series charts.
  • run-info.json: execution metadata, including the scenario, label, timestamps, k6 version, and container image.
  • scripts/: an exact copy of the scripts and scenarios used, allowing us to reproduce the test configuration even if the original files are modified later. #### Generated by the Report Lambda (GenerateReport):
  • metrics.json: metrics calculated by the code using the files generated during the test.
  • ai-analysis.json: the interpretation generated by Amazon Bedrock, along with the results of the numerical validation.
  • report.pdf: the final report, combining all the information above. To run a different test scenario, we only need to change the scenario value in the Step Functions execution input.

5.5. Report Generation

Once the test is complete, the pipeline processes the k6 results and generates a PDF report that combines the calculated metrics with an interpretation provided by Amazon Bedrock.
For this stage, we use an AWS Lambda function deployed as a container image, as we need several Python libraries: pandas for data processing, matplotlib for generating charts, and fpdf2 for creating the PDF document.

Unlike traditional ZIP-based deployments, which have a 250 MB uncompressed size limit, AWS Lambda supports container images of up to 10 GB. This makes it easier to package the code and its dependencies into a reproducible environment while maintaining a serverless execution model.

The following infographic summarizes the main benefits of this approach.


Illustration by the author. Based on AWS Lambda documentation.

The container image is built using a Dockerfile and pushed to Amazon ECR. Terraform then configures the AWS Lambda function to use this image, as illustrated in the following workflow.


Illustration by the author. Based on AWS documentation.

We can view an example of the generated PDF report at the following link:
github.com report.pdf


Report generated by the author using Python, Grafana k6, and Amazon Bedrock.

The report consists of several pages organized into the following sections:

  • Test Context: the executed scenario (load, duration, and thresholds) and the test environment (k6 version, container image, and location of the results).
  • Results and Metrics: requests, throughput, error rates, p50, p95, and p99 latencies, threshold compliance, and a breakdown of each phase of a request.
  • Performance Charts: response times over time, latency distribution, percentiles, request time breakdown, throughput, errors, and virtual users.
  • AI-Powered Analysis: an interpretation of the metrics generated by Amazon Bedrock, along with validation of the numerical values referenced in the analysis.
  • Metrics Glossary: definitions of each metric, how it is calculated, an example, and why it matters.

It is important to emphasize that all metrics are calculated using Python code based on the k6 results. Amazon Bedrock is used only to interpret these values and generate the narrative analysis, with an additional validation step to verify the numerical values mentioned in the generated text.

6. Conclusions

In this article, we started with a question: how does an API behave as concurrency increases? To answer it, we implemented an automated load testing pipeline that allows us to evaluate API performance under different load scenarios and analyze the results.

This exercise allowed us to put some Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) concepts into practice: defining which aspects of the service we want to measure (SLIs), establishing what service levels we consider acceptable (SLOs), and using Grafana k6 to translate those objectives into measurable thresholds during testing.

Beyond running load tests, we also need to interpret a considerable amount of performance data. To address this, we incorporated generative AI to facilitate the analysis and generate a report that summarizes the key findings without requiring an in-depth understanding of every metric. It is important to emphasize that the metrics are calculated by code, while AI is used only to interpret them, maintaining a clear separation between the collected data and the generated conclusions.

Another important aspect is the solution's reusability. By modifying the API, queries, and load testing scenarios, we can use the same pipeline to evaluate other services. In addition, preserving the configuration and results of each execution provides traceability and facilitates future comparisons.

However, this MVP has some limitations and opportunities for improvement:

  • Geographic Coverage: tests are executed from a single AWS Region, so they do not necessarily reflect the experience of geographically distributed users.
  • Test Duration: short test scenarios may produce limited sample sizes, which can affect the stability of percentiles such as p95 and p99.
  • AI Interpretation: the analysis depends on the model and prompt used. It would be interesting to evaluate different models and refine the instructions based on the type of insights we want to obtain.
  • CI/CD Integration and Observability: the pipeline is not yet integrated into a CI/CD process. As a future improvement, we could automate testing across application versions, compare results to detect performance regressions, and incorporate Amazon CloudWatch metrics for AWS Lambda and Amazon Bedrock.

Ultimately, the goal is not simply to determine how many requests an API can handle, but to establish a reproducible process that allows us to measure its behavior, identify potential performance degradation, and evaluate how its performance evolves as we introduce changes.

References

  • Beyer, B. et al. (2016). Site Reliability Engineering, capítulo 4: Service Level Objectives. https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/
  • Grafana Labs. (s. f.). Grafana k6. https://grafana.com/oss/k6/
  • Grafana Labs. (s. f.). Load test types. Documentación de Grafana k6. https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/testing-guides/test-types/
  • Amazon Web Services. (s. f.). Lambda quotas. Documentación de AWS Lambda. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html
  • Méndez Escobar, R. E. (2026). Identical or Similar? AI-Powered Product Matching with Amazon Bedrock and S3 Vectors. DEV Community. https://dev.to/aws-builders/identical-or-similar-ai-powered-product-matching-with-amazon-bedrock-and-s3-vectors-3pm

articles.title: 92 Green Field Tests Meant Nothing Until I Counted Which Could Lie
articles.description: The v0.2.0 field test for agentwatch ran 94 cases across 15 suites. 92 passed. 0 failed.  It was the...
articles.body_html:
The v0.2.0 field test for agentwatch ran 94 cases across 15 suites. 92 passed. 0 failed.

It was the least trustworthy green I'd ever shipped. Not because anything was failing — because I couldn't say why it was passing.

So I did a census. Of the 94 case assertions, how many could fail if the claim they were checking turned out to be false?

The answer was about 8.

The census

Every case had a step script. I read all 94 and sorted them into shapes:

Shape Count What it proves
Driver runs, prints ok: ..., exits 0 52 The commands executed
Container/service checks 16 The stack is up
Existence / syntax (test -f, json.tool) 11 The artifact exists and parses
Substring grep on own output 9 The word appears
python -c "import x" 5 The module loads
`... \ \ true`
Asserts a real condition ~8 The claim holds

That table is the whole finding. A suite where 8 of 94 assertions can fail isn't a test suite — it's a deployment script with extra steps. Every one of those 86 other cases would have stayed green with the feature broken, in many cases completely broken.

Two of the 92 greens were hiding exactly that: a Tempo backend that didn't exist, and a version banner that printed the wrong number. Both passed. Both were "plumbing green."

The method: four patterns, not 84 one-offs

Reading 94 cases sounds like a week of work. It was one evening, because the cases collapse into four patterns — and each pattern has one fix:

Pattern A — the shipped test already covers the plan condition. The single biggest surprise of the census: for something like 44 of the weak cases, the repo already had a canonical pytest module that asserts exactly what the field case was groping at. test_browser_verifier.py for the offline verifier, test_conformance_runner.py for the plugin API, test_access.py for the role matrix. The field case was doing test -f on a file while a real test sat two directories over.

The fix was one generic driver — shipped_tests.py, ~40 lines, which runs a named pytest module under the right PYTHONPATH and fails loudly if it doesn't pass. One driver, 44 cases grounded, zero re-implementation. If you take one thing from this post: before you write an assertion, grep your own test suite. The cheapest sufficient check usually already exists, and a hand-rolled one will drift from it.

Pattern B — the driver runs but its ok() is unconditional. The driver calls the real CLI, gets real JSON back, prints ok: ..., exits 0. Nothing ever looks inside the JSON. The fix is boring: parse it and assert the contract — the derivation version is present, the join summary carries the classified form, the statement is backed by a config key. The driver already had the data in its hand.

Pattern C — existence standing in for function. test -f verifier.html. json.tool bundle.json. import agentsec_agentwatch.conformance. Each of these has a real condition one step deeper, and each one got rewritten to it.

Pattern D — needs tooling that isn't in the room. Two cases need a real LangGraph SDK driver and two independent OSS parsers. No local fix exists. These stayed run-only, flagged, never faked — the report says "blocked" and names exactly what's missing. That's the fourth pattern's whole fix: honest labeling.

What grounding did to the failure count

Here's the uncomfortable, excellent part. Hardening didn't just make checks stronger — it made them fail. Three hardened cases went red on their first honest run:

  • A backend check that now queried Tempo — which was never started.
  • A matrix check that now asserted "no modeled Tier-1 rows" — one row was modeled.
  • A console accessibility check that now ran real axe rules — the page had no <main> landmark.

All three were product defects the old assertions couldn't see. Zero of them were test bugs. The green had been hiding them the entire time, and the only way any of them surfaced was by making an assertion able to fail.

That's the sentence I want to keep: you don't find bugs by running your suite, you find them by making your suite able to fail.

The bookkeeping that made it stick

Two small disciplines carried the campaign:

Every fix, re-run, before the report changes. Not "fixed in batch, verified later." One case, one run, one verdict on disk, then the report row updates. The report's totals are derived from verdict.json files, never from the summary JSON — stale summaries were exactly how earlier false greens hid.

A grounded/run-only tally in the report, not just PASS/FAIL. The final state reads 92 PASS / 0 FAIL / 1 declared / 1 N/A, and 90 of the 92 grounded. That second number is the one that took weeks. It's also the only number in the report I'd defend in an audit, because it's the only one with receipts per case.

Batches of 5, then 7 — same-shape cases together, one shared stack per batch, one commit per batch. Pattern-classification isn't just a reporting convenience; it's the difference between 84 one-off fixes and 4 fixes applied 84 times.

What I keep from this

  • A green suite answers "did it run." It takes deliberate work to make it answer "is it true."
  • Your repo's own test suite is the cheapest, least-drifty source of assertions. Grep it before writing any.
  • If a check can't fail, it will pass through anything — including the outage you wrote it to catch.
  • Blocked cases get labeled, not faked. The tally 90 grounded / 2 blocked is trustworthy because the 2 are named.

All of it is in the v0.2.0 field test report, shipped with agentwatch v0.2.1 — on PyPI.

The question worth taking to your own CI tonight: of your green suite, how many assertions could fail if their claim were false? If you don't know — that number is your suite's real size. Everything else is rehearsal.

References

  • Release: agentwatch v0.2.1 on GitHub · on PyPI
  • v0.2.0 field test report — the assertion-shape census, the four hardening patterns, and the per-case grounding tally
  • The generic driver that grounded 44 cases
  • The three defects hardening surfaced: FT-BACKEND-2 (Tempo), FT-MATRIX-1 (modeled Tier-1 row), FT-LUI-1 (console <main> landmark)
  • Suite: agentic-suite — the full set of agent-security tools

articles.title: How to Divide Work Across Threads in JavaScript: CPU Cores, Workload, and Smart Scheduling
articles.description: Modern applications often need to process millions of records, generate reports, analyze events,...
articles.body_html:
Modern applications often need to process millions of records, generate reports, analyze events, resize images, or perform complex calculations. As workloads grow, running everything on a single JavaScript thread can become a performance bottleneck.

The solution isn't simply to create more threads. The real challenge is deciding how many threads to create, how to divide the work, and how to assign tasks efficiently based on the machine's available resources.

In this guide, we'll explore how JavaScript multithreading works in Node.js, how to divide workloads across CPU cores, and how to design a worker system that can scale efficiently.

1. Understanding JavaScript's Execution Model

JavaScript traditionally executes application code on a single main thread. In Node.js, this thread runs the event loop, handles callbacks, and coordinates asynchronous operations.

Consider a program that processes a large dataset:

function processData(records) {
  for (const record of records) {
    // Perform expensive calculations
  }
}

processData(largeDataset);

If processData() performs CPU-intensive work, the main thread remains occupied until the function finishes. During that time, other JavaScript callbacks cannot execute on the same thread.

As a result, an application may become unresponsive, requests may take longer to complete, and overall throughput can decrease.

Node.js provides the worker_threads module to run JavaScript in separate threads. These workers can execute CPU-intensive tasks in parallel, subject to the machine's available CPU resources.

The important distinction is that asynchronous programming and multithreading solve different problems:

  • Asynchronous programming allows a thread to continue while waiting for operations such as network or file I/O.
  • Multithreading allows JavaScript code to execute on multiple threads, making parallel CPU computation possible.

Understanding this distinction is the first step toward building an efficient worker system.

2. How Does a Machine Determine Its Thread Capacity?

Before distributing work, we need to understand the machine running the application.

Imagine a server with the following specifications:

Resource Specification
Logical CPUs 8
RAM 16 GB
Workload CPU-intensive data processing
Main thread Handles coordination and application logic

The eight logical CPUs represent the hardware's reported capacity for simultaneous thread execution. Depending on the processor, logical CPUs may include simultaneous multithreading, such as Intel Hyper-Threading.

However, eight logical CPUs do not automatically mean that eight worker threads will produce the best performance.

Performance depends on several factors:

  • Whether the task is CPU-intensive or I/O-intensive.
  • How much memory each worker requires.
  • How much work is involved in creating and communicating with workers.
  • Whether other applications are competing for CPU resources.
  • Whether the application runs inside a container with CPU restrictions.

The operating system schedules threads across available processors. Multiple threads can exist even when fewer processors are available, but excess runnable threads may compete for CPU time.

Therefore, CPU count is a useful starting point for selecting a worker count, not a universal rule for determining the optimal number of workers.

3. Four Strategies for Dividing Work

There is no single strategy that fits every workload. The right approach depends on the shape of the data and the amount of computation involved.

Strategy 1: Divide work based on CPU availability

For CPU-heavy calculations, the number of available logical CPUs is a reasonable starting point.

Node.js provides os.availableParallelism() to estimate how much CPU parallelism the process can use.

const os = require("node:os");

const availableCPUs = os.availableParallelism();

const workerCount = Math.max(1, availableCPUs - 1);

console.log("Available CPU parallelism:", availableCPUs);
console.log("Initial worker count:", workerCount);

On a machine reporting eight available logical CPUs, this example starts with seven workers.

Leaving capacity for the main thread can be useful, but it is not always necessary or optimal. The main thread might perform very little CPU work, or the application might run alongside other services that require substantial resources.

Benchmarking should determine the final worker count.

Strategy 2: Divide work based on data size

Suppose an application needs to process one million records using four workers.

A straightforward approach assigns approximately 250,000 records to each worker.

The general formula is:

chunkSize = ceil(totalItems / workerCount)

This approach is known as static partitioning because the work is divided before processing begins.

It works particularly well when each item requires roughly the same amount of computation.

However, equal numbers of records do not always mean equal amounts of work. For example, processing a record with two fields may take far less time than processing one containing a large nested object.

When processing costs vary significantly, static partitioning can leave some workers idle while others continue working.

Strategy 3: Divide work into smaller tasks

Instead of assigning one large block to each worker, an application can divide the workload into smaller jobs.

For example, rather than assigning 250,000 records to each worker, it could create batches of 10,000 records.

Workers retrieve additional batches as they finish their current tasks.

This is dynamic scheduling.

It is particularly useful when:

  • Tasks have unpredictable execution times.
  • Records vary in complexity.
  • Some jobs occasionally fail or need retries.
  • The application processes a continuous stream of incoming work.

Dynamic scheduling introduces additional overhead for managing the task queue, so the batches should not be so small that coordination becomes more expensive than the computation.

Strategy 4: Divide work based on resource limits

CPU availability is only one constraint. Memory can become the limiting factor.

Suppose every worker needs 500 MB of additional memory for its data and intermediate calculations. Creating 20 workers could require roughly 10 GB of additional memory, before accounting for the main application, runtime overhead, and other processes.

A practical worker system should consider:

  • CPU availability.
  • Memory available to the process.
  • Input and output data size.
  • Queue length.
  • Task duration.
  • Other application activity.

Resource-aware scheduling is especially important in production services and containerized environments.

4. A Complete Example: Distributing Work Across Node.js Workers

Let's build a working example that calculates the sum of all integers from 1 to 100 million.

The goal is to divide the calculation into separate ranges, assign each range to a worker, and combine the results.

Project structure 

parallel-calculation/
├── main.js
└── worker.js

Step 1: Create the worker

Create worker.js:

const {
  parentPort,
  workerData
} = require("node:worker_threads");

const { start, end } = workerData;

let sum = 0;

for (let i = start; i <= end; i++) {
  sum += i;
}

parentPort.postMessage(sum);

Each worker receives a start and end value, calculates the sum of its assigned range, and sends the result back to the main thread.

Step 2: Create the main program

Create main.js:

const os = require("node:os");

const {
  Worker
} = require("node:worker_threads");

const TOTAL = 100_000_000;

const availableCPUs = os.availableParallelism();

// Choose a starting worker count
const workerCount = Math.max(1, availableCPUs - 1);

const chunkSize = Math.ceil(TOTAL / workerCount);

function runWorker(start, end) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const worker = new Worker("./worker.js", {
      workerData: { start, end }
    });

    worker.once("message", resolve);
    worker.once("error", reject);

    worker.once("exit", (code) => {
      if (code !== 0) {
        reject(
          new Error(`Worker exited with code ${code}`)
        );
      }
    });
  });
}

async function main() {
  console.log("Available CPUs:", availableCPUs);
  console.log("Workers:", workerCount);

  const jobs = [];

  for (let i = 0; i < workerCount; i++) {
    const start = i * chunkSize + 1;

    const end = Math.min(
      (i + 1) * chunkSize,
      TOTAL
    );

    if (start <= end) {
      console.log(`Assigning range ${start}-${end}`);

      jobs.push(runWorker(start, end));
    }
  }

  const results = await Promise.all(jobs);

  const totalSum = results.reduce(
    (total, result) => total + result,
    0
  );

  console.log("Final sum:", totalSum);
}

main().catch(console.error);

Step 3: Run the program

Install Node.js if necessary, then run:

node main.js

The program detects available CPU parallelism, calculates a chunk size, launches workers, and waits for all results.

The expected result is:

Final sum: 5000000050000000

The output also displays the CPU count, worker count, and assigned ranges.

This example demonstrates the essential workflow:

  1. Detect available CPU parallelism.
  2. Determine the worker count.
  3. Divide the input into ranges.
  4. Run the calculations in separate threads.
  5. Collect the results.
  6. Combine the partial results.

For this particular arithmetic problem, a direct mathematical formula would be much faster than either implementation. The example is intended to demonstrate work partitioning, not to suggest that creating workers is always the fastest solution.

5. Static Partitioning vs. Dynamic Scheduling

The previous example uses static partitioning: each worker receives a predetermined range.

Consider a different scenario where an application processes customer analytics events. Some events contain simple properties, while others require expensive transformations.

Assigning the same number of events to every worker might not produce balanced execution times.

A dynamic task queue can solve this problem.

Conceptually, the system works like this:

Incoming tasks
      |
      v
    Queue
   /  |  \
  v   v   v
 W1  W2  W3
  |   |   |
  +---+---+
      |
      v
  Completed results

Whenever a worker finishes its current task, it takes another task from the queue.

This approach is often called work sharing. It can improve utilization when task durations vary, although the queue itself must be designed to avoid becoming a bottleneck.

A production implementation might also include retry policies, cancellation, timeouts, task priorities, and backpressure to prevent incoming work from exceeding processing capacity.

6. Why Worker Pools Are Better Than Creating a Thread for Every Task

Creating a worker involves initialization, communication setup, and resource allocation. If an application creates a new worker for every small task, this overhead can become significant.

A worker pool keeps a fixed number of workers alive and reuses them for multiple tasks.

For example, a pool might maintain four workers:

Worker pool
├── Worker 1 → Task A → Task E
├── Worker 2 → Task B → Task F
├── Worker 3 → Task C → Task G
└── Worker 4 → Task D → Task H

Tasks can wait in a queue until a worker becomes available.

A worker pool can provide:

  • Controlled concurrency.
  • Reduced worker initialization overhead.
  • More predictable resource usage.
  • Centralized error handling.
  • Better throughput for repeated CPU-heavy jobs.

In Node.js, worker pools can be implemented using worker_threads or libraries such as Piscina.

The pool size should still be selected according to the workload and measured performance.

7. How to Find the Optimal Number of Workers

Suppose a workload runs on a machine reporting eight available logical CPUs.

You could benchmark it using different worker counts:

Worker count What to evaluate
1 Baseline performance
2 Benefit from initial parallelism
4 Throughput and CPU utilization
6 Additional scaling
7 Potential balance with main-thread work
8 Whether using all available parallelism helps

Measure the time required to complete the same workload, as well as throughput, CPU utilization, memory usage, and latency.

For a CPU-intensive task, adding workers can reduce execution time until the workload becomes limited by processor capacity, memory bandwidth, synchronization, or other overhead.

Beyond that point, additional workers may offer little improvement or even reduce performance.

Also remember that worker threads are not independent physical CPUs. They share the machine's underlying resources, and CPU scheduling can affect their performance.

The best configuration is the one that meets your performance goals within your resource budget.

8. Common Mistakes to Avoid

Creating too many workers

More workers do not always mean faster execution. Excessive concurrency can increase memory consumption and scheduling overhead.

Assuming every task takes the same time

Equal-sized chunks work best when processing costs are reasonably uniform. For uneven tasks, dynamic scheduling can improve load balancing.

Using workers for ordinary I/O operations

Network requests and many file operations can already be handled asynchronously by Node.js. Workers are most valuable when substantial CPU-intensive JavaScript work would otherwise block the main thread.

Ignoring data-transfer costs

Workers normally communicate using messages, which can involve copying data. Large data transfers can offset the benefits of parallel computation. Transferable objects and shared memory can help in appropriate cases, but they require careful ownership and synchronization.

Ignoring memory limits

Every worker adds runtime overhead and may allocate its own data. A worker count that works on a development laptop might be inappropriate in a production container with less memory or CPU capacity.

9. Final Architecture: A Resource-Aware Worker System

For a production application, a robust design generally combines several of these techniques:

  1. Detect the available CPU parallelism.
  2. Establish a configurable upper limit for workers.
  3. Estimate the memory and processing cost of tasks.
  4. Divide work into appropriately sized batches.
  5. Use a worker pool to reuse threads.
  6. Use dynamic scheduling when tasks vary significantly in duration.
  7. Measure throughput, latency, CPU usage, and memory consumption.
  8. Adjust the configuration based on observed performance.

The result is a system that distributes work according to both the machine's capabilities and the workload's characteristics.

Conclusion

Multithreading is not just about creating more threads. It is about distributing work efficiently across the resources available to your application.

CPU-based partitioning provides a useful starting point. Data partitioning works well for uniform workloads. Dynamic scheduling helps balance uneven tasks, while resource-aware limits prevent excessive CPU and memory consumption.

For JavaScript developers, Node.js worker_threads provides the foundation for parallel CPU-intensive execution. Combining it with chunking, worker pools, and performance measurement can turn a single-threaded bottleneck into a more scalable processing system.

The key principle is simple: choose the worker count based on available resources, divide work according to its computational cost, and let real performance measurements guide optimization.

articles.body_html:
Overview

Before architecture, implementation, and deployment comes a question that can ruin an otherwise excellent planning meeting: does this artifact need to exist at all? Everybody has already agreed on the repository name. It feels unkind to bring reality into it now.

An Apple Is a Ridiculous Amount of Work

An apple is a deceptively small achievement. You walk into the kitchen, pick one up, wash it if you are feeling responsible, and eat the outer two-thirds. Perhaps you navigate around a bruise. Perhaps you leave a heroic centimetre of perfectly good apple attached to the core because getting closer would require an awkward rotation and a level of commitment you did not bring to lunch. Then you throw the rest away, having successfully consumed the part for which you believe the entire arrangement exists.

To produce those six bites, the world first had to grow a tree. Not an apple dispenser with a convenient trunk attached, but roots, bark, branches, leaves, blossoms, and a reproductive strategy involving third parties with wings. The tree requires water, soil, microbes, suitable weather, and years of sunlight. The pollinators require other plants and somewhere to live. Somewhere downstream are farmers, refrigeration, trucks, grocery stores, and a teenager putting the Honeycrisps in the wrong bin again. The apple costs three dollars because nobody has itemized the universe.

Then your body extracts a relatively small amount of useful energy and material through a digestive system you have been operating your entire life without once scheduling a dependency upgrade. The energy eventually becomes motion, thought, bodily maintenance, and heat. It does not remain in an internal apple battery. Eating one at age seven does not settle the matter through retirement, although a subscription service would certainly advertise the possibility.

At first glance, this looks like staggering waste. We grew an orchard, involved the bees, transported the fruit, and maintained an entire organism so that I could stand over the kitchen sink and decide the remaining bit was too difficult. But the accounting is suspiciously centered on me, which is often where suspicious accounting begins.

The seeds are not manufacturing defects. From the tree's perspective, they may be the principal deliverable, while the flesh is a marketing expense incurred to persuade an animal to distribute them. The leaves are not unnecessary because I decline to eat them. The roots are not overhead that an ambitious tree startup can eliminate in version two. What looks disposable from one position may be essential from another; the tree has not agreed that my snack is its corporate mission.

The apple is the visible result at the tip of an enormous dependency cone. This does not establish that apples are a mistake. It establishes that looking at the fruit is a poor way to estimate what makes fruit possible, which brings us, regrettably, to software.

Every Tool Requires a World

A small software tool looks cheap. One repository, six source files, a build configuration, and a README containing an example that worked on the author's laptop on the afternoon it was written. The implementation took two days. Someone posts a rocket emoji, whose exhaust does not appear in the estimate.

Unfortunately, source code is only the trunk. The tool needs tests, releases, packages, documentation, compatibility decisions, and somebody who remembers why it behaves differently on Tuesdays. Depending on what it does, it may also need authentication, authorization, networking, monitoring, deployment automation, and a Kubernetes cluster. We began with a command that rearranges a string and have arrived at a staffing question.

Users learn it. Applications integrate it. Pipelines call it. Other systems generate its inputs and interpret its peculiar outputs. People write wrappers because the interface is almost right, then wrappers around those wrappers because the first wrappers belong to another department and changing them requires a meeting. The repository remains admirably small. The meetings have not been committed to it.

A tree offers an inconvenient illustration of how this happens. If a large tree weighs tonnes and grows out of the ground, why is there not a tree-sized hole underneath it? Where did the material come from? I admit this question troubled me longer than it should have. The ground appeared to have supplied a tree while remaining entirely ground, which would be an impressive procurement arrangement.

Most of a tree's dry mass is built from material acquired through the air, especially carbon from carbon dioxide, rather than bulk soil hauled upward through the roots. The tree gains substance from something surrounding it that we usually do not notice. Water makes up much of its living weight as well; the point is not that soil contributes nothing, but that looking for a missing tree in the dirt misunderstands the transaction.

Tools acquire mass from their surroundings too. A flag becomes part of a deployment procedure. An output column enters a finance report. A bug becomes something every consumer compensates for, after which correcting it is called a breaking change. Somebody learns that retries must occur exactly three seconds apart and teaches the next person, without either of them finding this requirement in the code. The implementation is visible and countable. The dependency on it has become atmospheric.

Creation starts at the center and moves outward, one enthusiastic adopter at a time. Removal starts at the edges, except nobody knows where the edges are. You think you are deleting a program. Six months later, a report fails because a cron job still calls version 1.3 from a server everyone believed had been decommissioned in 2019. The server is named temp-final-2, which is not a name so much as a record of negotiations lost.

The useful accounting therefore includes creation, integration, operation, adaptation, and eventual extraction. These are categories, not independent quantities in a reassuring equation: changing the interface can increase integration cost, refusing to change it can increase operating cost, and making either choice without knowing the consumers can increase everyone's blood pressure. The original implementation estimate describes the part whose author was present to estimate it.

Creation is paid by the team making the decision. Integration is paid by adopters. Operations are paid by whoever gets paged. Extraction is paid years later by people who were not in the meeting and would like to know why a temporary command now participates in financial reporting. The ticket has been archived, the documentation returns 404, and the original team has achieved the only reliable form of decoupling: employment elsewhere.

Construction Has Excellent Visibility

Most engineering advice begins after the decision to create has already been made. Here is how to build a service, select a framework, structure a repository, and make the result observable, secure, reusable, extensible, and deployable across seventeen regions. We receive extensive guidance on maintaining the thing and remarkably little pressure to establish why there should be a thing to maintain.

Even advice against complexity tends to accept construction as the default. “Keep it simple” means build a simpler artifact. “You aren't gonna need it” removes optional features from the artifact we have already authorized. “Do not repeat yourself” sometimes replaces three repeated lines with forty-seven lines of abstraction, making the repetition disappear into a place where nobody can comfortably inspect it. “Reuse before build” may import someone else's dependency cone, release schedule, design assumptions, and newly creative interpretation of licensing.

None of these principles is useless, and several can reject the whole proposed artifact when taken seriously. We have a remarkable talent for applying them only after approving the repository. Under that interpretation, you can follow all of them faithfully and produce an exemplary system whose main accomplishment is giving six people something else to remember.

Artifacts are easy to recognize as work. We can count commits, pull requests, repositories, services, and launches. When morale deteriorates sufficiently, we can count lines. A requirement eliminated by one awkward question leaves much less evidence. There is no service to demo, no migration to announce, and no incident dashboard showing the failure mode that never existed. The engineer who prevented the project appears to have spent the week talking.

This is how construction passes for engineering: it leaves something we can point at. Restraint leaves a smaller invoice, a quieter pager, and an empty space in the architecture diagram that somebody will eventually propose filling. The savings are distributed. The absence of a launch is immediately visible to the person assembling the quarterly presentation.

The distinction also matters to the Neo-Fermi/Wilson AI paradox. If implementation output is abundant, we still need to ask where that abundance becomes a worthwhile outcome. More software is evidence that software was produced. Whether it improved the situation remains a separate investigation, usually scheduled after the celebration.

The Question Before the Ticket

The ordinary sequence is to build something that works, improve it, make it efficient, and remove whatever turns out to be unnecessary if there is still time. There is never still time. By then, applications depend on it, dashboards measure it, and somebody has colored it “strategic” in the roadmap. The unnecessary part now has stakeholders, which is how a technical fact acquires legal representation.

The sequence needs to begin earlier. Prevent an unnecessary obligation before taking it on; examine obsolete obligations before preserving them; build what survives the inquiry and make it work correctly. That may be a demonstrated necessity or a bounded experiment whose potential benefit warrants its cost, not merely another object approved because nobody could prove it useless. This is an order of inquiry, not an instruction to perform speculative deletions while everyone waits for a payment to settle. An existing component may need to remain during migration, and a necessary new one may need to arrive before the old one can leave. Reality is annoyingly unwilling to execute a manifesto in numbered order.

The Zeroth Law of Engineering is therefore: do not build what need not exist.

It comes before architecture, implementation, testing, and deployment because those activities cannot retroactively justify their own subject. A perfectly functioning unnecessary system may be harder to remove than a broken one. People will trust it, adopt it, and eventually describe its continued existence as a requirement.

A request usually arrives as a proposed object. “We need a dashboard” sounds settled until you discover that someone needs to know whether a process completed. “We need a database” may mean two executions must share one small piece of state. “We need a microservice” may mean nobody wants responsibility for a function already in the application. The named artifact conceals the actual constraint while giving the meeting something to estimate.

Swimming upstream means asking what happened, what outcome is required, and what prevents the existing arrangement from producing it. Sometimes the capability already exists. Sometimes a rule can change. Sometimes the report nobody reads can stop being produced, taking its proposed dashboard with it. Occasionally you still need the database, and now you have the rare pleasure of knowing what it is for before selecting one.

This is not a request to optimize a needless process until it becomes too impressive to cancel. In the fan-noise essay, reducing work and questioning its continuation are different moves. An engineer can spend six weeks making a job cheaper while carefully avoiding the person who could confirm that its final consumer stopped using it last February. The job becomes efficient. February remains unconsulted.

The Bamboo Has Not Read the Label

I own a PVC pipe cutter that I use to cut thick bamboo in my backyard. I do not believe I have ever cut PVC with it. The cutter seems untroubled by this departure from its stated career path, which is more than can be said for many people who discover their degree is not a physical law.

“PVC pipe cutter” is a market category. The relevant mechanism is a ratcheted shearing action suited to certain cylindrical materials. Bamboo can fit that mechanical contract without fitting the label. Searching for a bamboo-specific artifact would have been understandable and might have produced a very attractive purchase, but the bamboo would not have been cut any more convincingly.

The famous Knuth–McIlroy word-frequency example makes a similar distinction. Knuth wrote a substantial program as a demonstration of literate programming. McIlroy showed how existing Unix commands could compose the required transformations: split text into words, normalize, sort, count, rank, and select. One approach demonstrated how a program could be constructed and explained; the other demonstrated how the task could be expressed using capabilities already present.

They were serving different purposes. A teaching artifact does not become unnecessary merely because there is a shorter way to produce its output. If the requirement is to demonstrate literate programming, the program is doing work the pipeline is not. If the requirement is to count words, however, the pipeline deserves examination before we commission another executable and someone inherits its release process.

The useful alternative to bespoke software is not automatically one enormous tool with nine hundred flags. Nor is it a sixty-stage shell pipeline relying on accidental whitespace, locale-sensitive sorting, and a regular expression whose author disappeared from a forum in 2008. That is a custom program written sideways, with its dependency declarations distributed across your hopes.

What matters is whether the essential transformations already exist behind contracts stable enough for the job. Composition still needs validation, ownership, and an explanation of what happens when a stage fails. The absence of a new repository does not mean the absence of a new obligation. A pipe cutter can cut bamboo; it cannot make judgment unnecessary.

Let's Cook, Claude

A missing comma can move Claude from the person being addressed to the object of the sentence, which is a troubling start to a production specification. I mean “Let's cook, Claude,” although even that leaves open whether we are preparing dinner, generating a deployment system, or producing another metaphor about toast. Natural language is impressively flexible until flexibility enters the acceptance criteria.

Generative AI makes the Zeroth Law more important because it makes creation easier without settling necessity. Ask for a helper and you may receive a helper, an interface, a configuration layer, a test suite, and a cheerful README introducing the project to a world that had managed quite comfortably without it. The model is responding to the request. The request has already decided what success should look like.

If the first attempt fails, we ask it to continue. A local problem becomes a framework because frameworks offer more places to put the next correction. Soon there are agents coordinating agents, a custom message broker, and eleven pans on the stove. We originally wanted toast, but toast has become the reference implementation of our breakfast platform.

The economic change is real. A developer who expected an abstraction to take two weeks might spend an hour searching for an existing capability. When the abstraction can be generated in thirty seconds, searching feels like the expensive option. This comparison is persuasive only if the story ends when generation ends. Unfortunately, the compiler has no authority to close the account.

Generated code still needs to be understood, reviewed, secured, tested, operated, upgraded, and eventually removed. It can produce the visible trunk quickly. Consumers, operational assumptions, compatibility demands, and failure modes do not become free because the first draft arrived before the coffee. The pull request contains four thousand lines, nine interfaces, and documentation explaining why all nine interfaces are necessary. Two other models agree. We have achieved independent agreement about an assumption nobody asked them to challenge.

The useful prompt begins before implementation. Ask the model to recover the outcome behind the requested artifact, inspect the repository for existing capability, compare safe compositions, and consider whether obsolete behavior can be removed. Then ask for the smallest change that survives that inquiry, including its consumers and how it could later be replaced. This is less exciting than watching a service materialize, but excitement has never been a reliable compatibility policy.

AI can assist with search, comparison, impact analysis, and subtraction. It can also get those wrong, which is why “the model found no consumers” is a finding to investigate rather than permission to delete production state. The objective is not to replace construction with confidently automated non-construction. It is to stop rewarding output before determining what output would help.

Practice Without Starting a New Practice

“Build nothing” cannot mean refusing useful work while reciting philosophy in sprint planning. Sometimes the existing tool is dangerous, inaccessible, expensive, or incapable of meeting the requirement. Sometimes a new capability creates possibilities worth exploring before there is a mature business case. The law asks creation to survive examination; it does not require the future to submit receipts before arriving.

Begin by describing the outcome without naming the proposed apparatus. A person needs to know within five minutes when an event fails. That is a constraint. A notification service is one possible response, not yet a fact about the universe. An existing alert might satisfy it. Changing the process might remove the failure. Or the service might genuinely be needed, in which case we can discuss delivery guarantees instead of spending the first week naming notification abstractions.

Adoption must become discoverable. If nobody can find the consumers, nobody can confidently estimate the thing's mass or remove it safely. That may require usage records, explicit dependency declarations, or simply ownership that survives a team reorganization. These mechanisms also cost something. An inventory platform for three scripts can reproduce the problem it was commissioned to solve, now with a nicer search box.

Finding those consumers lets us ask what they actually depend on. Ideally, it is behavior we intend to preserve, not the particular order of an accidental output or the fact that a timeout currently returns success. Once enough consumers adapt to a bug, the bug receives tenure. Correcting it still matters, but now correction includes migration rather than a triumphant one-line patch and an afternoon of surprise.

That migration problem is why the exit belongs in the entrance discussion. Who will know when the last consumer has left? Can implementations coexist during replacement? Who owns extraction after the original team moves on? A tool without answers becomes a future Chesterton's fence, surrounded by people who suspect it is unnecessary but have discovered that suspicion is not a rollback plan.

For an experiment, the extraction problem can start before anyone admits there is a product. A proof of concept is scaffolding, not a constitutional amendment, and it needs a point at which somebody decides whether it continues. Its expiry should trigger review, not an unattended deletion while consumers are using it. If it succeeds, keep the parts the evidence supports. If it fails, remove it before a copied example becomes somebody else's reason that removal is impossible.

Subtraction also needs to count as work. An architecture review can ask which obligations disappear, and a planning discussion can recognize an avoided migration as an outcome rather than a missing deliverable. Otherwise the rational career move is to build the thing, become its indispensable expert, and later receive recognition for managing the complexity one introduced. This need not involve bad intentions. The incentives are capable of arranging it without assistance.

Most importantly, distinguish support from waste. Tests, documentation, observability, and migration paths are not leaves we can remove because customers only eat the fruit. If the tool must exist, responsible support may be part of its irreducible cost. The Zeroth Law is not a discount code for shipping unsupported software. It is a reason to consider that cost before promising the object at the tip of the cone.

The harder question is whether we can allow a needless process and its corresponding demand to cease. Engineers are good at improving execution, preserving compatibility, and retaining just in case. Ceasing asks us to relinquish something we know how to manage, perhaps something we built ourselves. It may also ask us to admit that a very successful quarter produced a very maintainable obligation.

First, Build Nothing

Tools are made from tools, just as ideas are made from ideas. Every artifact inherits languages, protocols, libraries, infrastructure, and accumulated knowledge. Once adopted, it changes what later systems can assume. A convenient output becomes an input somewhere else; an experiment becomes a precedent; a workaround becomes the example used to train the next engineer. Every tool is both fruit and seed, including the ones we were quite sure would remain internal.

This is why creation is not local and removal is not deletion. Deleting the repository can leave its historical data, contracts, procedures, and expectations alive elsewhere. The thing may be gone while everything still holds its shape. We have removed the apple dispenser and retained an organization that arrives every morning carrying a bowl.

Engineering begins by looking beyond the visible artifact to the conditions it requires and the conditions it will create. Build when the actual constraint warrants it. Make the result correct, support it honestly, and preserve a practical way for it to stop existing. But before turning a request into another part of the world, leave room for the possibility that no new part is required. An empty repository is not necessarily an unfinished project; sometimes the question was answered before it needed one.

Postscript: The Tree Makes an Objection

I confess I have rarely encountered a proper postscript in an actual letter outside literature, so this is quite exciting. It is also necessary because the tree remains standing after the argument, still producing apples with an apparent disregard for my excellent concerns about its architecture.

The tree pays much of its growth cost before producing fruit repeatedly. It can shelter animals, feed pollinators, stabilize soil, and create more trees. Some of what appeared to be overhead supports several outcomes at once. The dependency cone is large, but the returns do not stop at my six bites over the kitchen sink. I was not wrong to notice the cost. I was wrong if I thought noticing it completed the evaluation.

The tree would have had difficulty passing a conventional architecture review before its first apple. Years of growth, underground dependencies, seasonal availability, third-party pollination, and a deliverable whose principal consumer discards the reproductive payload: please simplify and resubmit. A procurement team might recommend buying apples instead, thereby moving the tree outside the diagram and announcing that the dependency had been eliminated.

This is the limit of the law. A dependency cone reveals the scale and character of an investment; it does not prove the investment should never be made. Some artifacts are valuable because they enable outcomes nobody could fully specify beforehand. Their uncertainty should be acknowledged, their continuation examined, and their support funded, rather than treated as either permission for everything or an argument for nothing.

Do not build what need not exist, but do not confuse “I cannot yet justify this” with “this need not exist.” Aggressive restraint can prevent useful compounding just as enthusiastic construction can produce permanent housekeeping. The question is not how to avoid ever being wrong. It is how to make a decision whose benefits, obligations, and grounds for reconsideration remain visible after the rocket emoji has scrolled away.

The tree can stay. I am less certain about the dashboard that reports whether the tree is still there, but apparently three teams consume it now.

This essay was written and revised with the help of AI. No new service was required, although a Markdown file did survive examination.

articles.body_html:
A workflow fails. I fix the configuration and click Execute Node.

But what should happen next?

The selected node might depend on three upstream nodes. One succeeded, another produced incomplete data, and the third hasn't run at all.

Should the engine rerun everything? Reuse previous results? Wait for missing inputs?

These questions turn a seemingly simple debugging operation into a problem of dependency analysis, execution-state reconstruction, and data consistency.

While exploring n8n's execution engine, I became interested in how it handles this problem, particularly when partial executions interact with nodes that receive multiple inputs.

Consider an example of a workflow I created

If Generate report fails, restarting the entire workflow might repeat unnecessary API calls or external side effects. Running only that node, however, may fail because its required inputs are unavailable.

The engine must reason about three separate things:

  • The Graph topology
  • Its Execution history
  • Its Execution eligibilty

The workflow's execution state changes with every run.

Partial execution is a state-reconstruction problem

Partial execution allows developers to run a selected portion of a workflow instead of repeating the entire process.

The challenge is deciding which previous results can be reused and which dependencies must be evaluated again.

Data stored in execution history isn't always valid for subsequent runs—upstream parameters can change, and past contexts can drift.

Recomputing everything wastes resources; reusing everything risks incorrect results.

Similar to incremental computation that is recalculating only what changed, workflow engines face extra complexity because nodes trigger external side effects, call APIs, and follow split data paths.

Ultimately, the core problem isn't just deciding which node to run, but determining which execution state is valid to reach that node safely.

Why multi-input nodes complicate scheduling

Here's a node that combines customer data with order data in this workflow

A simplified scheduler might assume that a node is ready when all its parents have executed. Real execution semantics are more complicated.

An upstream node might have executed but returned zero items. Another might not have executed at all. A third might be waiting for data from another branch.

Scheduling cannot always be reduced to checking whether a node's immediate parents have run.

Inside n8n's execution engine

A useful starting point for investigating this behaviour is the WorkflowExecute implementation in n8n's core package:

workflow-execute.ts.

Two areas are particularly interesting.

1) Its Execution Stack

The engine tracks scheduled node work and processes nodes as execution progresses. After a node produces output, the engine must inspect its outgoing connections and determine whether downstream work is ready.

Consider this flowchart 

A ["Select runnable node"] --> B["Prepare inputs"]
B --> C["Execute node"]
C --> D["Record output"]
D --> E{"Downstream node ready?"}
E -->|Yes| F["Schedule node"]
E -->|No| G["Wait for required input"]
F --> A
G --> A

This is a conceptual representation, not a complete reproduction of n8n's internal implementation.

The important detail is that producing output and scheduling the next node are separate responsibilities.

2) Reconstructing partial execution

The same file contains runPartialWorkflow2, which provides a concrete entry point for examining partial workflow execution.

At a high level, this path involves resolving a destination, identifying a relevant subgraph, accounting for existing run data, and preparing the execution stack and waiting input state.

The goal is to execute the required portion of the workflow without blindly replaying unrelated operations.

This introduces a correctness requirement: the engine must select the appropriate nodes and supply them with the appropriate data and context.

Exploring the n8n repository and going through its PRs

I explored a few n8n pull requests and came across #10758, titled “fix(core) handle nodes with multiple inputs and partial data correctly during partial executions.”

The PR basically ensures nodes with multiple inputs(like a merge node) handle data correctly during partial workflow execution.

And why is this an interesting engineering problem?

During partial execution, a Merge node might have some upstream data ready while other inputs are still pending. The engine's job is to figure out if it has enough context to safely schedule the node.

While a Merge node shows the problem, the real challenge is with execution scheduling and state reconstruction.

To look into this, I'd check:

  • The exact code changes.
  • Edge-case test coverage.
  • Review the notes on execution-stack reconstruction.
  • The PR status (currently marked as a Draft, so it's a proposed idea, not a finished fix).

The main takeaway? Features like partial execution, multi-input nodes, and saved execution data work fine on their own, but keeping their logic intact when they interact is where things will get tricky.

A deeper lesson

This investigation connects workflow automation to several broader concepts:

Incremental computation: Recalculating only the work affected by a change.

Data provenance: Preserving information about where data originated and how it reached a node.

Scheduling: Determining which operations are eligible to execute next.

State consistency: Ensuring that reused execution data remains appropriate for the current run.

Observability: Making enough execution information available to investigate failures and reproduce behaviour.

These concerns are tightly connected. A scheduler can select the correct node but still produce an incorrect result if it supplies stale or incomplete inputs.

A workflow debugger is therefore more than a visual editor. It is also a tool for inspecting and manipulating execution state.

Conclusion

The more I explored partial execution, the less I saw it as a convenience feature and the more I saw it as a test of the execution engine's underlying model.

The challenge is not simply to execute fewer nodes. It is to execute the correct subset of nodes with the correct inputs and the right interpretation of prior state.

Multi-input nodes expose this complexity particularly well because they force the engine to reason about dependencies, data availability, and execution history together.

That is what makes workflow engine development interesting. Correctness often depends on the interactions between features, not just on whether each feature works independently.
