articles.title: Your console.log() Might Be Slowing Down Your App
articles.description: Most of us use console.log() every day.  Checking an API response? console.log().  Debugging a loop?...
articles.body_html:
Most of us use console.log() every day.

Checking an API response? console.log().

Debugging a loop? console.log().

Trying to figure out why something isn't working? Another console.log().

It's one of the simplest debugging tools in JavaScript. But there's something we often overlook: logging isn't free, and too much of it can affect performance.

Let's understand why and how to avoid it.

First, what is the Console API?

The Console API gives us methods to print messages, inspect values, and debug our applications.

Some commonly used methods are:

Method Purpose
console.log() Print general messages
console.info() Display information
console.warn() Show warnings
console.error() Report errors
console.table() Display data in a table
console.time() Measure execution time

Here's a simple example:

const user = { name: "John", age: 25 };

console.log(user);
console.table([user]);
console.warn("Something needs attention!");

Nothing complicated, right?

But here's an interesting detail.

console isn't actually part of the JavaScript language itself.

Who provides console? JavaScript or the browser?

JavaScript follows a specification called ECMAScript.

That specification defines things like variables, functions, objects, arrays, and promises.

But it doesn't define console.

Instead, console is provided by the environment where JavaScript runs.

  • Browsers provide it through their developer tools.
  • Node.js provides its own console implementation.
  • Other runtimes can implement it differently.

That's why console behavior and performance can vary between environments.

The problem: Logging inside loops

Imagine you're processing 10,000 records.

While debugging, you add a simple log:

const records = Array.from(
  { length: 10_000 },
  (_, index) => index
);

for (const record of records) {
  console.log(record);
}

Looks harmless.

But this loop doesn't just process 10,000 records. It also asks the runtime to handle 10,000 logging operations.

Depending on the environment, those operations may involve formatting values, passing messages to developer tools, or writing output.

And all that work takes time.

How much slower can it get?

In one local test, the results looked like this:

Test Measured time
Single console.log() call 0.003 ms
1,000 calls inside a loop 26.4 ms

These are example measurements, not universal benchmarks. Actual results depend on the browser, runtime, machine, output size, and whether DevTools is open.

The important point is simple:

A tiny cost repeated thousands of times can become noticeable.

And even if your browser groups repeated messages into one line, it doesn't mean the logging calls were skipped.

How can we avoid this?

The good news is that we don't need to stop using console.log().

We just need to use it carefully.

1. Remove unnecessary logs

Debug logs are useful while developing, but most don't need to stay in production.

Instead of:

for (const user of users) {
  console.log("Processing:", user);
  processUser(user);
}

Keep it simple:

for (const user of users) {
  processUser(user);
}

If you need to know how many users were processed, log a summary instead of every individual record.

for (const user of users) {
  processUser(user);
}

console.info(`Processed ${users.length} users`);

One useful message is often better than thousands of repeated messages.

2. Create a simple logger

If you frequently debug your application, a small logger can help.

const isDevelopment =
  process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production";

export const logger = {
  log: (...args) => {
    if (isDevelopment) {
      console.log(...args);
    }
  },

  warn: (...args) => {
    if (isDevelopment) {
      console.warn(...args);
    }
  },

  error: (...args) => {
    console.error(...args);
  },
};

Now use it anywhere:

logger.log("User loaded successfully");
logger.warn("Response is taking longer");
logger.error("Failed to load user");

In production, debug messages won't be printed.

Just remember that calling a no-op logger still has a small cost, especially if you're calculating expensive values before passing them to it. Also, process.env.NODE_ENV must be supported or replaced by your build tool.

3. Remove console calls during the build

If your project uses Terser, you can configure it to remove console statements when building for production.

For example:

// vite.config.js
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  build: {
    minify: "terser",
    terserOptions: {
      compress: {
        drop_console: ["log", "debug", "info"],
      },
    },
  },
});

This removes the selected console methods from the production bundle.

Notice that we haven't removed console.error().

That's intentional.

One important thing: Don't blindly remove every console call. Some messages are useful for troubleshooting real production issues. Build-time removal can also remove argument expressions, so avoid relying on side effects inside logging calls.

4. Keep important error reporting

Not every console message is unnecessary.

For example:

try {
  await saveUser(user);
} catch (error) {
  console.error("Failed to save user:", error);
}

Errors are worth recording.

For larger production applications, a proper logging or error-monitoring system is even better. It helps you understand failures without depending entirely on browser console output.

Just make sure you don't accidentally log passwords, tokens, or sensitive user information.

A small habit that makes a difference

console.log() isn't bad.

It's incredibly useful, and there's no reason to avoid it while debugging.

The problem starts when we leave unnecessary logs in frequently executed code, especially loops, rendering logic, and high-traffic paths.

A few things worth remembering:

  • Avoid logging every iteration of a large loop.
  • Remove unnecessary debug messages before production.
  • Use a simple logger when it makes sense.
  • Configure your build tools to strip unwanted logs.
  • Keep meaningful error reporting.

You probably won't notice a performance difference from removing two or three logs.

But removing thousands of unnecessary logging operations from a hot path? That can make a real difference.

The takeaway: Use the console to understand your code, not to slow it down.

Have you ever found unnecessary console.log() calls causing performance issues in a project?

I'd love to hear about it! 👇

articles.title: Vue v-for: The Directive Unmounted Hook Bug, Fixed in 3.5.41
articles.description: A custom directive's unmounted hook could silently skip firing inside a keyed v-for list. The directive unmounted hook bug, Vue's real fix, and a cheat sheet.
articles.body_html:
You write a custom directive once — v-tooltip, v-click-outside, v-ripple — attach something in mounted(), tear it down in unmounted(), and trust the pair like you'd trust addEventListener/removeEventListener. Then you drop it onto a row inside a filterable v-for list. Filter an item out. No error. No warning. The row disappears from the screen — and on some Vue 3 versions, unmounted() never ran. The listener it attached is still live, attached to a DOM node nothing references anymore. This was a real bug in Vue's own compiler, open for years, fixed only in Vue 3.5.41 — and understanding why it happened teaches you more about how v-for actually works than the fix note ever will.

What You'll Learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain why a custom directive's lifecycle hooks can be skipped for an element inside v-for, even though the same directive works fine outside a loop
  • Reproduce the symptom, confirm whether your installed Vue version is affected, and verify the fix
  • Describe what a compiler patch flag is and why NEED_PATCH specifically matters for refs, vnode hooks, and custom directives
  • Write directive-based cleanup you can trust inside a list, instead of discovering the gap in production
  • Tell this bug apart from unrelated v-for gotchas (duplicate keys, index-as-key) that look similar but have different causes

Who this is for: you've written a custom directive with app.directive() or a local directives option, and you've used v-for with :key. If directives themselves are new to you, the Vue Guide to Custom Directives is worth reading first — this article assumes you know what mounted/unmounted hooks are, not how to write your first one.

Table of Contents

  • The Problem: A Cleanup Hook That Sometimes Doesn't Run
  • The Mental Model: Patch Flags Decide What the Runtime Bothers to Visit
  • The Bug, the Issue, and the Fix
  • Edge Cases and Gotchas
  • Best Practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat Sheet
  • Key Takeaways

This is written against Vue 3.5.x (verified 3.5.43, current on npm's latest tag as of this writing). Vue 3.6 is still a release candidate (3.6.0-rc.10 on the rc tag) and isn't stable yet, so nothing here depends on it. The fix this article covers shipped in Vue 3.5.41, released August 5, 2026 — if your package.json pins anything older, you are likely affected (one of the two issues the fix closed was filed against 3.2.47, so this isn't a 3.5-only gap).

The Problem: A Cleanup Hook That Sometimes Doesn't Run

Say you've written a small directive that logs its own lifecycle — a stand-in for anything real a directive might do (attach a listener, instantiate a third-party widget, start an observer):

<!-- the directive — nothing unusual about it -->
<script setup>
const vLog = {
  mounted(el, binding) {
    console.log(`mounted: row ${binding.value}`)
  },
  unmounted(el, binding) {
    console.log(`unmounted: row ${binding.value}`)
    // in real code: removeEventListener, destroy a tooltip instance,
    // disconnect an observer — whatever mounted() set up
  },
}
</script>

Used on a single element, it behaves exactly as documented: one mounted log when it appears, one unmounted log when it's removed. Now put the same directive on an element inside a keyed v-for, and remove an item from the middle of the list by filtering the underlying array:

<template>
  <div v-for="row in visibleRows" :key="row.id" v-log="row.id">
    {{ row.label }}
  </div>
</template>

// remove row 2 from the data the list is built from
visibleRows.value = visibleRows.value.filter(r => r.id !== 2)

On an affected Vue version, row 2's <div> disappears from the DOM exactly as expected — but the console only ever shows the mounted log for it, never unmounted. Nothing throws. Nothing warns. The directive's cleanup code simply never executes for that element, while the identical directive on a non-looped element works every time. That asymmetry — directive hooks are reliable alone, unreliable in a v-for — is the entire bug, and it's what makes it so easy to ship without noticing: your manual test on one element passes, and the loop case only misbehaves once a list gets edited in production.

The Mental Model: Patch Flags Decide What the Runtime Bothers to Visit

The mental model: at compile time, Vue's template compiler inspects every element and decides which ones are worth revisiting when the component re-renders. An element with no dynamic text, no bound class, no bound prop — nothing that could ever change — gets compiled as fully static, and the runtime skips it entirely on every future patch. That skip is most of why Vue is fast: it never diffs what it already knows can't change.

To make that work, the compiler attaches a patch flag to every dynamic element — a small integer bitmask recording which kind of dynamic content it has: TEXT for interpolated text, CLASS/STYLE/PROPS for bound attributes, and so on. The runtime reads the flag instead of diffing blindly, so it only compares the parts of the vnode the flag says can change.

Now consider an element that has no dynamic text or props at all — only a ref, a v-bind to a vnode hook, or (as in the example above) a custom directive. Nothing about its rendered output ever changes, but Vue still needs to visit it on every patch, because a ref needs updating, a vnode hook needs calling, or a directive's updated/unmounted hook needs invoking at the right moment. That's exactly what the NEED_PATCH flag exists for: it tells the runtime "nothing here looks different, but visit it anyway — something non-visual depends on it."

The bug was that NEED_PATCH could get dropped specifically when that same element was also inside a v-for. The compiler's own v-for-specific optimizations and its patch-flag analysis for refs/hooks/directives didn't compose correctly, so an element that would have correctly carried NEED_PATCH on its own lost that flag once it was also a loop child. Without the flag, the runtime had no signal telling it to visit the element during a patch — so the directive's lifecycle hook for that specific element silently went uninvoked.

The Bug, the Issue, and the Fix

This wasn't a hunch — it's two tracked issues and a merged fix in Vue's own repository. Issue #12569, titled "Custom directive's unmounted event is not triggered on v-for element," reported exactly the symptom above. Issue #9239 reported the same underlying gap for ref callbacks on v-for children — the flag loss wasn't directive-specific, it affected every NEED_PATCH-only case: refs, vnode hooks, and custom directives alike.

The maintainer who fixed it, in PR #11682 ("preserve vnode lifecycle in stable v-for"), described the bug precisely: "When an element uses ref, vnodeHook, or custom directives, the patchFlag should be NEED_PATCH. However, when they are used together with v-for, the patchFlag gets lost." The fix tracks whether an element needs patching separately from whether it needs to stay a full "block" in the compiler's internal tree, and the v-for transform now adds NEED_PATCH back wherever one of these lifecycle-sensitive features is present. It shipped in Vue 3.5.41 (2026-08-05).

What that means for you in practice: if your package.json resolves vue to 3.5.41 or later — or anything on the current 3.5.43 — this is already fixed, and the example above behaves correctly: both mounted and unmounted fire for every row, every time. If you're pinned to an older 3.5.x release, or anywhere earlier in the Vue 3 line (one of the two issues this fix closed, #9239, was reported against 3.2.47), the gap is real and silent. The straightforward fix is upgrading to 3.5.41 or later; this article doesn't catalog a non-upgrade workaround, since the bug lives in the compiler's static analysis rather than in anything your component code controls — check the linked GitHub issues directly if you need to stay pinned for now.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

This is not the index-as-key bug. A separate, much more famous v-for mistake — using the array index as :key — causes Vue to reuse the wrong DOM node and misattribute state across reorders. That's a key-strategy problem you control by choosing a stable :key. The bug in this article happens even with a perfectly correct, stable :key — it's a compiler flag that was lost, not a key you chose wrong.

v-if and v-for on different elements of the same loop are unaffected. This specifically concerned "stable" v-for — a keyed loop with no structural directive (v-if/v-for) on the same element changing the number of children per iteration independent of the list itself. Combining v-for with v-if on the same tag is already discouraged by Vue's own style guide, and can throw a runtime reference error if the v-if expression depends on the v-for's loop variable — a separate, unrelated problem, not this bug.

Built-in reactive bindings were never affected. v-model, v-show, bound :class/:style/props, and interpolated text all carry their own patch flags (PROPS, STYLE, CLASS, TEXT) regardless of v-for. The gap was specific to elements whose only dynamic feature was a ref, a vnode hook, or a custom directive, with nothing else forcing a patch flag already.

ref callbacks silently missing inside v-for was the same bug. If you've ever seen a ref array (:ref="(el) => refs.push(el)") inside a loop skip an entry or hold a stale element after a list changed, issue #9239 describes the identical mechanism — not a separate problem to debug.

Custom directives using only created/beforeMount/beforeUpdate hooks were affected identically to mounted/unmounted. The bug was about the patch flag being present at all, not about which specific directive hook fires — every hook on the affected element went uninvoked on the patches where the flag was missing.

Best Practices

Reach for this knowledge when you maintain any directive that does real cleanup — removing listeners, destroying a third-party widget instance, disconnecting a ResizeObserver or MutationObserver — and that directive is ever used inside a list. Confirm your installed Vue is 3.5.41 or later before trusting that cleanup unconditionally.

Avoid relying on directive lifecycle hooks for anything correctness-critical even after upgrading. Directives are the right tool for DOM-only side effects (focus management, third-party widget wiring, scroll/intersection observers) — not for application state that must be perfectly consistent, where a watch or computed-driven reactive update gives you a mechanism entirely outside the compiler's patch-flag analysis.

Write a real regression test for list-cleanup directives, not just a manual click-through: mount a list with the directive, remove an item, and assert the directive's unmounted hook actually ran for it. This bug shipped silently for years precisely because it only reproduces once an item leaves a loop — a test that only ever mounts, never removes, would never have caught it.

Pin and read your Vue version deliberately, especially on a long-lived app. npm ls vue (or checking the lockfile) tells you exactly what you're running; npm view vue dist-tags tells you what's current. A multi-year-old pin anywhere before 3.5.41 is exactly the situation this bug could still be lurking in.

FAQ

Why didn't Vue throw an error or a dev-mode warning for this?

Because nothing about the element's own rendering was wrong — the DOM node itself unmounted correctly along with its parent list item. The only thing missing was Vue's internal signal to also invoke the directive's hook on that specific vnode. There was no incorrect state for Vue to detect and warn about; the gap was an omission in the compiler's static analysis, not a runtime contradiction it could catch.

Does this affect v-model or other built-in directives?

No. v-model compiles to a bound prop plus an event listener, both of which already carry their own patch flags (PROPS) independent of this bug. The gap only touched elements whose sole dynamic feature was a ref, a vnode hook, or a custom directive with nothing else forcing a patch flag.

Is Nuxt affected the same way?

Yes, to the extent any given Nuxt app's resolved vue dependency was on an affected version — Nuxt renders on top of Vue's own core, so this is a Vue-core fix, not something Nuxt layers on. Check vue's resolved version in your Nuxt project's lockfile the same way you would in a plain Vue app.

Is this fixed in Vue 2?

Not applicable — Vue 2's compiler doesn't use this patch-flag/block system at all (it was introduced with Vue 3's rewritten renderer), so the bug and its fix are both Vue-3-specific.

How do I confirm my own app isn't exposed?

Check your resolved vue version (npm ls vue), and if it's below 3.5.41, reproduce the repro in this article in a scratch component before deciding whether to upgrade immediately or schedule it — a directive that only logs, with no real side effect, costs nothing to leave broken; one that owns a listener or a third-party instance is worth fixing promptly.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 9-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

Cheat Sheet

Task What to check Notes
Confirm you're affected npm ls vue Affected: any Vue 3 release before 3.5.41 (reported as far back as 3.2.47)
Confirm you're fixed Vue ≥ 3.5.41 (current: 3.5.43) No flag, no config — the fix is purely internal
Reproduce the symptom Custom directive + keyed v-for + remove an item Log mounted/unmounted; on affected versions only mounted appears
Tell it apart from index-as-key bugs Does it happen with a correct, stable :key? This bug happens even with a correct key; index-as-key is a separate mistake
Root cause, one line NEED_PATCH patch flag dropped for ref/vnode-hook/directive-only elements inside v-for vuejs/core#11682
What's NOT affected v-model, bound :class/:style/props, interpolated text These already carry their own patch flags regardless of v-for 
// A directive you can trust inside v-for, once Vue is ≥ 3.5.41:
const vCleanupCheck = {
  mounted(el, binding) {
    el.__cleanup = () => console.log(`cleaned up row ${binding.value}`)
  },
  unmounted(el, binding) {
    el.__cleanup?.()
  },
}
// Regression-test it: mount a list, remove an item, assert unmounted ran.

Key Takeaways

  • A custom directive's mounted/unmounted hooks could silently fail to fire for an element inside a keyed v-for, with no error or warning — fixed in Vue 3.5.41.
  • The cause was a compiler detail: elements whose only dynamic feature is a ref, a vnode hook, or a custom directive need the NEED_PATCH flag to be visited during a patch, and that flag could get lost specifically when combined with v-for.
  • This is unrelated to the index-as-key mistake — it happened even with a correct, stable :key.
  • If you maintain a directive that does real cleanup, confirm your Vue version is 3.5.41 or later, and write a test that actually removes a list item rather than only mounting one.

The listener nobody was tracking is the quiet failure mode that makes this bug worth knowing even now that it's fixed: it never crashed, never logged a warning, and would have kept accumulating in a long-running single-page app for as long as the affected Vue version stayed pinned. Compiler-level bugs like this are rare, but they're exactly why "it works when I click it once" isn't the same as "it works" — the loop is where cleanup earns its keep.

Have you run into a directive that seemed to stop working only inside a list, or found another case where NEED_PATCH mattered? Drop it in the comments.

articles.description: I built a calorie tracker. It's called ForkCount. It's free. There's no card, no trial, no "start...
articles.body_html:
I built a calorie tracker. It's called ForkCount. It's free. There's no card, no trial, no "start your 7-day free trial" wall, and no premium tier hiding the barcode scanner behind $12.99/month.

I'm 13. I can't write JavaScript from memory. I built it using Google AI Studio — describing what I wanted, testing what came back, fixing what broke. Two weeks of debugging. It's live now.

What it does

Shows you the math. Most apps give you a number. ForkCount gives you the number and the formula behind it — your BMR, your TDEE, your activity multiplier, your goal adjustment. Every step is visible. If you want to know why your target is 1,400 and not 2,000, the app tells you.

Calculates from your body, not an average. Mifflin-St Jeor for BMR, Katch-McArdle if you know your body fat percentage. Then activity level, then goal. The target is yours, not a default.

Logs food by typing. "200g chicken and 150g rice" parses to two items with macros. No searching a database for each ingredient. Type it, log it.

Weekly meal plans that use your target. Not a generic 2000 kcal plan. Your calorie target. Your dietary preference. If you're vegetarian, the plan is vegetarian.

Tracks water, weight, and exercise. Water in glasses, weight in trends, exercise with kcal burned.

Runs in your phone browser. No download. No app store. Open the link, sign up, done.

What it doesn't do

  • No food photo scan (in progress)
  • No barcode scanner (removed after it kept misfiring — it's coming back when it works)
  • No Apple Health / Google Fit sync
  • No verified nutrition data for anything not in the built-in list
  • No premium tier, because there's no business model. It's just free.

Why I built it

Every calorie app I tried wanted a card before it showed me anything useful. The math was always hidden. The target was always a black box. The "free" version was always a trial, or an ad-supported version of a paid app, or a version that locked the one feature you actually needed behind a subscription.

So I built one that doesn't do that. The math is visible. The target is yours. The app is free.

Why I'm posting

I want to know if the calorie math is right. If you've tracked long enough to know your real TDEE, run the onboarding and compare. If the number ForkCount gives you is off by more than 100 kcal, tell me how and I'll fix it. If it's right, tell me that too — I need to know the calculator works before I trust it.

I also want to know what's missing. What feature do you use in MyFitnessPal that you can't live without? What would make you switch? Not "add every feature" — what's the one thing?

Try it

https://forkcount.github.io

Free. No card. No trial. Works on any phone browser. Two weeks old, so there will be bugs — but every bug I hear about gets fixed within a day.

If you try it and something breaks, tell me what you were doing and what phone you're on. I read every message.

Built with React, Vite, Supabase, and a lot of patience. Deployed on GitHub Pages. If you're building something similar and want to know how the Supabase migration went, ask in the comments — I'll write it up.

articles.title: FableCut Gets its Own Studio Which Agents Can Actually Use
articles.description: I've been building FableCut for the past few months, and one thing I've wanted to explore is what...
articles.body_html:
I've been building FableCut for the past few months, and one thing I've wanted to explore is what video editing looks like when an AI agent can work directly with the editor instead of just generating instructions for a human to follow.

The idea is straightforward: open a video editor, connect an AI agent, describe the edit you want, and let the agent make changes to your actual project.

That project is now FableCut Studio.

Studio: https://studio.fablecut.space/

GitHub: https://github.com/ronak-create/FableCut

Here's a quick demo of FableCut Studio in action:

What is FableCut?

FableCut is an open-source video editor designed to work with AI agents through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

The project started as a local editor that agents could control through project.json and MCP. The first version shipped on July 6, 2026.

Since then, I've shipped 20 tagged versions, made 383 commits, and grown the project to 747 GitHub stars and 86 forks. It's available on npm as fablecut, is listed in the official MCP registry, and has been included in awesome-mcp-servers.

The original version required a local installation. Studio takes the same idea into the browser.

You open a link, load a project, connect an agent, and start editing.

No editor installation is required.

Why let an AI agent control a video editor?

Most AI video tools focus on generating a new video from a prompt. I wanted to explore something different: letting an agent work with an existing editing timeline.

Imagine giving an agent instructions like:

  • Cut every occurrence of "you know" from this recording.
  • Caption this reel in a highlight style.
  • Remove the pauses from this take.
  • Adjust the color grading of this shot.
  • Export the final video in a vertical format.

These tasks involve more than generating a video. The agent needs to understand the project, make targeted changes, and preserve the existing work.

That's the direction I've been building toward with FableCut.

How Studio works

Studio runs at https://studio.fablecut.space/ and exposes 16 tools through remote MCP.

Different clients can connect to it, including Claude Code, claude.ai, Cursor, ChatGPT, OpenCode, and other compatible MCP clients.

The connection process depends on the client. For example, claude.ai supports a custom connector, while Claude Code can connect using a command.

Once connected, the agent can call tools to inspect and modify the project. Those changes appear live in the editor.

There's also an Agent panel that lists tool calls, and you can pause the agent or issue a new link when needed.

The important part is that the agent isn't simply returning a list of suggestions. It's interacting with the actual editing project.

What happens to the files?

In Chromium-based browsers such as Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Arc, Studio can work with a folder on your disk and save project.json there.

Firefox and Safari use browser storage for projects, with a download option for exporting the project as a ZIP.

Your video clips are not uploaded to Studio's server.

There is one important distinction: the remote MCP relay carries tool calls and their results, including project information and any frames the agent requests. It does not receive the media files themselves.

I think being clear about this boundary matters when building AI tools that work with local files.

What's new in v1.17?

The latest release adds transcription and text-based editing to Studio.

These features make it possible to perform common editing tasks using the words spoken in a video rather than manually searching through the timeline.

1. Transcription directly in the browser

Studio uses Whisper to transcribe audio in the browser.

The model is approximately 77 MB and downloads the first time transcription is used. After that initial download, transcription runs on the device.

In one desktop CPU test, 48 seconds of speech took 13 seconds to transcribe.

That is a useful result for a feature that doesn't require uploading the audio to a transcription service.

2. Editing videos through text

Once a transcript is available, you can interact with the words directly.

You can click a word to jump to its position, select words and delete them, or search for a phrase and cut every occurrence in one operation.

The cuts are grouped into a single undo step, making it easier to experiment without losing control of the edit.

For example, if a recording contains several repetitions of the same phrase, you can remove those repetitions without manually locating each one on the timeline.

3. Word-by-word captions

Studio can generate captions from the transcript and time them word by word.

The available styles include:

  • Subtitle
  • Karaoke
  • Highlight, where the currently spoken word changes color
  • Word pop

Caption layouts also adapt to the canvas dimensions, so vertical videos can use narrower lines than landscape videos.

SRT and VTT import and export are supported as well.

4. Silence removal

Studio can automatically remove pauses from a recording.

This is useful for talking-head videos, tutorials, interviews, and short-form content where long pauses can make the final video feel slow.

One limitation worth mentioning: Whisper generally drops filler words such as "um" and "uh". Silence removal and transcript-based editing serve different purposes, so filler removal is better handled through the silence-removal workflow rather than assuming every filler will appear in the transcript.

5. Agents can use these features too

The transcription and editing features aren't limited to manual use in the browser.

Agents can use tools such as fablecut_transcribe, fablecut_captions, and fablecut_silence.

That means a prompt like "caption this reel in highlight style" can become an actual editing operation instead of a tutorial explaining how to create captions.

This is where I think MCP becomes particularly useful: it gives an agent a structured way to interact with an existing application.

There's more than speech editing

The project has grown well beyond basic timeline operations.

Over the last several releases, I've added:

  • Advanced editing: source monitoring, ripple and roll edits, track targeting, markers, and typed timecode.
  • Audio tools: mixer buses, effect chains, automation, loudness normalization, auto-ducking, crossfades, and noise reduction.
  • Color grading: waveform monitoring, RGB parade, vectorscopes, color wheels, curves, and HSL adjustments.
  • Compositing: masks, track mattes, and motion tracking.
  • Motion graphics: shape layers, parenting, motion paths, motion blur, text on a path, and animation presets.
  • Media management: metadata search, offline relinking, proxies, delivery presets, and batch export.
  • Project management: multiple sequences, version history, and faster exports through WebCodecs.

These features matter because an agent needs a real editing environment to work with. The more capable the editor becomes, the more useful its tools can be.

Agents can also inspect frames, measure color grades using scopes, and save project versions before substantial edits. The editor respects track locks rather than treating the entire timeline as freely editable.

Exporting without sending your video to a server

Studio encodes exports in the browser, supporting formats and codecs including H.264, HEVC, VP9, and AV1, with supported audio options.

WebCodecs has also helped make exports substantially faster. In v1.16, the project introduced an export path measured at roughly five times faster than the previous implementation.

For an editing application, performance matters just as much as the AI integration. An agent might make the right changes, but the workflow is still frustrating if exporting the result takes too long.

What if you prefer running everything locally?

Studio isn't the only way to use FableCut.

You can install the local version through npm:

npx -y fablecut

The local version exposes 21 MCP tools and supports additional machine-local workflows, including FFmpeg-dependent features.

This is a useful option if you prefer a local agent setup or need functionality that isn't available in the browser version.

Try it yourself

I've added a demo project containing skate clips, a music track, and an initial edit. You don't need to prepare your own footage just to see how the editor works.

  1. Open FableCut Studio.
  2. Load the demo project.
  3. Connect a compatible AI agent.
  4. Try asking it to caption the video or remove pauses.

You can also explore the source code on GitHub.

FableCut is released under the MIT license.

What's next?

I'm continuing to build FableCut around the idea that AI agents should be able to work inside real creative applications, with structured tools and visible results.

There's still plenty to improve, but the latest release brings the project closer to a workflow where an agent can help with the tedious parts of editing while the editor remains the place where the actual project lives.

If you try it, I'd genuinely like to hear what works, what breaks, and what you'd want an agent to be able to do next.

articles.title: My VS Code setup went from 47 extensions to 6. My productivity went up.
articles.description: I counted my VS Code extensions. There were 47. My editor took 8 seconds to start, lagged when I...
articles.body_html:
I counted my VS Code extensions. There were 47. My editor took 8 seconds to start, lagged when I typed, and crashed once a week. I disabled 41 of them and kept 6. Here is what happened.

The problem

Extension creep is gradual. You install a formatter, then a linter, then a theme, then a snippet pack, then a language support extension for a framework you tried once and never used again. Each one seems small. Each one adds startup time, memory usage, and editor complexity.

My 47 extensions included:

  • 5 formatters (Prettier, ESLint, Stylelint, Beautify, Rustfmt)
  • 4 language packs (Python, Go, Rust, Java, only Python was active)
  • 3 themes (one in use, two installed "to try later")
  • 6 snippet packs (React, Vue, Python, Docker, Git, and a generic HTML one)
  • 4 Git extensions (GitLens, Git Graph, GitHub Pull Requests, Git History)
  • 3 AI extensions (GitHub Copilot, Codeium, Tabnine, all disabled in favor of Cursor)
  • 22 others (Docker, YAML, TOML, markdown preview, CSV viewer, path intellisense, import cost, indent rainbow, bracket pair colorizer, and more)

Most of these I had installed once and forgotten about. They were running on every startup, consuming memory, registering commands, and contributing to the status bar.

What I kept

I went through each extension and asked: "Have I used this in the last week?" If the answer was no, I disabled it. Here is what survived:

1. Prettier. Code formatting. I use it on every file. Non-negotiable.

2. ESLint. Linting. Same as Prettier, I use it constantly. The two work together.

3. GitLens. I use the blame and diff features daily. The rest of GitLens (code lens, file history, commit search) I could live without, but the blame view alone justifies the extension.

4. Astro. Language support for Astro, which is my primary framework. Without it, .astro files are unstyled HTML.

5. Tailwind CSS IntelliSense. Autocomplete for Tailwind classes. I write Tailwind every day. Without this, I am guessing at class names.

6. Error Lens. Shows errors and warnings inline instead of requiring a hover. It is a small UX improvement that saves me hundreds of micro-interactions per day.

That is it. Six extensions.

What happened

Startup time: 8 seconds to 1.5 seconds. The difference is immediately noticeable. I open and close the editor many times a day, and the 6.5 second saving compounds.

Memory usage: 1.2 GB to 380 MB. VS Code went from being the heaviest application on my machine to being lighter than my browser. The lag when typing in large files disappeared.

Crashes: once a week to zero in six weeks. I cannot prove causation, but the correlation is strong. Extension conflicts are a known cause of VS Code instability, and removing 41 of them eliminated a lot of potential conflicts.

Productivity: up, measurably. I was spending time managing extensions: updating them, configuring them, disabling ones that conflicted, and debugging issues caused by interaction between them. That time is gone. The editor does what I need and gets out of the way.

What I learned about extension creep

Extensions are not free. Each one adds to startup time, memory footprint, and editor complexity. The cost is invisible until you remove them and feel the difference.

You do not use most of your extensions. 41 out of 47 had not been used in the last week. Some had not been used in months. They were running anyway.

The best extensions are the ones you forget you have. Prettier, ESLint, Error Lens: these work silently. They do not have popups, side panels, or status bar clutter. They do their job and disappear.

AI extensions are redundant when you use an AI editor. I was running Copilot, Codeium, and Tabnine inside VS Code while also using Cursor (which has its own AI). The AI extensions were disabled but still loaded. Removing them freed memory and removed a source of confusion about which AI was active.

The 2026 editor landscape

The choice in 2026 is not "which extensions should I install." It is "which editor should I use." The landscape:

  • VS Code remains the default. The extension ecosystem is the largest. With a minimal setup, it is fast and reliable.
  • Cursor is VS Code with AI built in. If you are paying for an AI assistant, Cursor replaces the need for AI extensions.
  • Zed is the performance option. Rust-native, fast startup, built-in collaboration. Smaller extension ecosystem.
  • JetBrains (WebStorm, IntelliJ) is the heavy option. Built-in tooling for everything, but higher memory footprint and per-seat licensing.

My current setup is Cursor (which is VS Code under the hood) with the same 6 extensions. The AI features are built into the editor, so I do not need AI extensions. The 6 extensions I kept are the ones that do work the AI cannot do: format my code, lint it, show Astro syntax, autocomplete Tailwind classes, and display errors inline.

If you want to try this

  1. Open your extensions tab. Sort by "installed."
  2. For each extension, ask: "Have I used this in the last week?"
  3. Disable everything where the answer is no. Do not uninstall yet, just disable.
  4. Work for a week. If you need an extension you disabled, re-enable it.
  5. After a week, uninstall everything that is still disabled.
  6. Measure your startup time before and after. The difference is your motivation to keep it lean.

The temptation to install will return. Every blog post about "10 VS Code extensions you must have" will add to your list. The discipline is not "never install." It is "install, try, and remove if you do not use it within a week."

articles.title: JSON.parse Source Text Access: Stop Losing Precision on Big IDs
articles.description: JSON.parse can now hand your reviver the original source text of every number, and JSON.rawJSON lets you write it back out exactly. Here's how to round-trip 64-bit IDs and decimals without string hacks.
articles.body_html:
Your API returns an order ID of 9007199254740993. Your frontend logs 9007199254740992. Nobody touched it. JSON.parse quietly rounded it, because every JSON number becomes a JavaScript double, and doubles only hold integers exactly up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (9007199254740991). Anything bigger gets snapped to the nearest representable value before your code ever sees it.

The usual workarounds are all a little sad. Ask the backend to send IDs as strings (id_str, if you remember the old Twitter API). Pull in a third-party parser like json-bigint. Or run a regex over the raw response to wrap long numbers in quotes before parsing, and hope nothing in a string field looks like a number. The platform now has a real fix: the JSON.parse source text access proposal, which adds a context argument to revivers and a matching JSON.rawJSON() for serialization. It reached Stage 4 at TC39 in late 2025, and it is already Baseline: Chrome 114, Firefox 135, Safari 18.4, Node 21, Deno 1.33, and Bun 1.1.43 all ship it.

The reviver gets a third argument

A reviver has always received (key, value). It now receives (key, value, context), and for primitive values context.source is the exact slice of JSON text that produced value. The number was still parsed into a lossy double, but you get the original digits next to it, so you can decide what it should become.

const json = '{"orderId": 9007199254740993, "total": 42.5}';

const order = JSON.parse(json, (key, value, context) => {
  if (key === "orderId") {
    // value is already rounded; context.source is not
    return BigInt(context.source);
  }
  return value;
});

order.orderId; // 9007199254740993n
order.total; // 42.5

Keying off property names works when you control the schema, but a generic version is more useful in a shared fetch helper. Promote only integers that actually lost precision, and leave everything else alone:

const INTEGER = /^-?\d+$/;

export function preciseReviver(key, value, context) {
  if (
    typeof value === "number" &&
    !Number.isSafeInteger(value) &&
    context?.source &&
    INTEGER.test(context.source)
  ) {
    return BigInt(context.source);
  }
  return value;
}

const res = await fetch("/api/orders");
const data = JSON.parse(await res.text(), preciseReviver);

Two details there matter. Response.json() doesn't accept a reviver, so you read the body as text and parse it yourself. And the optional chaining on context?.source is deliberate: context.source only exists for primitives. When the reviver is called for an object or array, source is absent, because there's no single meaningful slice of text to give you once the children have already been revived.

Writing it back out with JSON.rawJSON

Parsing is half the problem. Hand that BigInt to JSON.stringify and you get TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt. Convert it to a Number first and you're back to rounding. JSON.rawJSON() closes the loop: it wraps a piece of JSON text that stringify will emit verbatim.

function preciseReplacer(key, value) {
  return typeof value === "bigint" ? JSON.rawJSON(value.toString()) : value;
}

JSON.stringify({ orderId: 9007199254740993n }, preciseReplacer);
// '{"orderId":9007199254740993}'

The output is a real JSON number, not a quoted string, so a Go or Java backend expecting an int64 reads it without any schema change. JSON.rawJSON is strict about what it accepts: the text must be valid JSON for a primitive, so JSON.rawJSON('[1, 2]') or a string containing a raw line break throws a SyntaxError. The returned object is frozen with a null prototype, and JSON.isRawJSON() tells you if you're holding one.

Decimals, not just big integers

Money is the other place this pays off. 0.1 parsed as a double is not exactly one tenth, and a payments API that returns "amount": 19.99 hands you a value that's already slightly wrong before your decimal library sees it. With context.source you can feed the original digits straight into whatever arbitrary-precision type you use:

import Decimal from "decimal.js";

const invoice = JSON.parse(body, (key, value, context) =>
  key === "amount" ? new Decimal(context.source) : value,
);

On the way out, JSON.rawJSON(amount.toFixed(2)) writes 19.99 as an unquoted number again.

When not to reach for it

A reviver runs once per value in the document, so it is measurably slower than a plain JSON.parse on large payloads. If your IDs are already strings, or every number fits in the safe range, you don't need any of this. In TypeScript, older lib definitions may not know about the third reviver argument or JSON.rawJSON yet, so you might need a small ambient declaration until your lib setting catches up. For older browsers, core-js ships a polyfill for both halves.

The bigger change is where the fix lives. Precision used to be something you negotiated with the backend team or patched with a dependency. Now it's a few lines in the one fetch helper every request already goes through. MDN's pages on JSON.parse() and JSON.rawJSON() have the full reference, and the TC39 proposal covers the design reasoning.
